speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT RESPECTING OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 2 I announced in the house certain steps being taken by the government and certain proposals being made to the provinces with respect to offshore mineral rights. At the same time I issued maps showing the location of mineral resource administration lines off the east and west coasts, and stated that similar lines would also be drawn in the regions of Hudson Strait, Hudson Bay and James Bay, together with a line defining the boundary between submerged lands adjacent to the provinces and those adjacent to the Northwest Territories and Arctic islands.
I am pleased to announce today that these lines have now been drawn, and I am issuing at this time a map showing their location.

As stated in my earlier announcement, the federal government will continue to administer and manage the mineral resources on the seaward side of the mineral resource administration lines. The coastal provinces are being offered the opportunity to administer all the offshore mineral rights on the landward side of these lines, and the federal government is prepared to concede to them the revenues -derived therefrom. Furthermore, should this proposal prove acceptable to the provinces, we would in addition be disposed to place half the revenues accruing from the mineral resources seaward from these lines in a single national pool to be shared among the provinces on some basis acceptable to them.

I have sent to the Premiers a copy of today's statement as well as the new mineral resource administration lines map for the 29180-391
Hudson Bay-Hudson Strait region. I have been pleased with the general response thus far to my announcement of December 2. In particular, a number of oil companies are now proceeding with major programmes of exploration offshore and they seem to have obtained the necessary confidence to do this from the positive statement of federal policy. I hope and believe that we should now be able to work out with the provinces the details of financial and other arrangements to implement these proposals.

Hear, hear.

Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, this matter, of course, has a considerable background in terms of federal-provincial relations. The government of Canada sought a legal opinion from the Supreme Court of Canada on the legal rights to minerals off the west coast of the country. The government of Canada having announced it was proceeding with this reference, there were discussions of the matter at federal-provincial conferences at that time. The then Prime Minister of Canada gave the provinces the assurance, upon the legal opinion being obtained, that the question of offshore mineral rights would thereafter be discussed with the provinces.
Therefore, there are two questions that immediately occur to anyone. The first question is whether the legal decision with regard to rights off the west coast is equally appropriate to the offshore rights off the east coast. There are a number of provinces that have argued very vigorously that this is not the case. The legal position regarding mineral rights under Hudson Bay is, of course, recognizably in a quite different category. I do not think the provinces have ever claimed any legal right to the minerals under Hudson Bay.

I am convinced that the result of that breach will

be a further cteterioriation in the relations between the federal government and some provinces. subtopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT RESPECTING OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's proposal seems a reasonable basis for negotiations. However I cannot help wondering if that statement was made without any prior consultations with the provinces; or is it the result of consultation with the provinces, and is this proposal their general consensus of the matter?
It seems to me that matters of this sort that have been the subject of controversy for a considerable period really cannot be settled by pronouncements from the throne. They ought to be settled by negotiations and discussions, in order that some consensus may be reached that is acceptable to the federal and provincial governments. If the provinces have not been consulted, then I hope the Prime Minister's statement is merely the basis for discussion rather than a final decision. I also hope the Prime Minister will be prepared to go one step further and tell us how this matter may be dealt with in a practical way. Unfortunately pools of oil and mineral deposits know nothing about lines drawn on maps. Often the only way to develop these resources is to unitize an entire oil field or mineral deposit. Joint action by the federal and provincial governments may be necessary to unitize an area in order that it can be developed to the maximum extent. I therefore hope the government will be prepared to sit down with the provinces and discuss the unitization of mineral and oil resources. I also hope that as the result of today's statement the Prime Minister and his ministers will follow up this matter so that some agreement may be reached. The matter has been long outstanding and the sooner a settlement acceptable to all parties concerned is reached, the sooner the areas in question will be developed.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening the Minister of Transport outlined to the committee some views regarding housing and the report of the task force on housing. One very pertinent question we must ask ourselves when we consider the views expressed by the minister is: In what capacity was the minister speaking to us last night? Was he speaking to us as a spokesman for the government announcing government policy? I think the clear answer to that question is that he was not. He was merely explaining to the committee his views as chairman of the task force on housing.
Let me say immediately that I agree with a good many of the recommendations of the task force. I have to, because a good many of them seem to have been taken from the election program of the Progressive Conservative party in the last election. I want to be very frank this afternoon, without in any way being abusive, and tell the minister that his explanation to the committee was really of very little use. We have no way of knowing how many of the views expressed by the minister may become government policy. We have no way of knowing which of these views will be adopted by the government. We have no way of knowing which views will actually be recommended by the minister to the government.
I must say quite frankly through you, Mr. Chairman, that the position of the minister at this juncture is simply not credible. First of all, the Prime Minister has placed the minister in an absurd position. For some time prior to the publication of this report the minister was boasting about his revolutionary program. He boasted about how he was going to cut red tape and get ahead with the housing program. But the Prime Minister, as has become his practice in some instances, proceeded to cut the feet from under the minister.
I should like to quote one or two remarks made by the Prime Minister in this connection. In the house on February 14, as reported at page 5525 of Hansard, the Prime Minister made the following statement:
Until the constitution is brought into the 20th century in some of these respects-
March 4, 1969

He was referring to housing policy and urban renewal programs.
governments are to a large degree powerless to solve the problems either by acting alone or in co-operation with other levels of government.
There we have a very clear statement by the Prime Minister that it is to a large degree impracticable for the governments of this country, either alone or in co-operation with each other, to deal with the housing problem in Canada. Thus a curious state of affairs has been created. On the one hand we have the Minister of Transport boasting of how he is going to get the program moving under the present constitution, boasting of how he is going to cut red tape. On the other hand the Prime Minister rises in the house and says that to a large degree the governments of the country, presumably including this government, are powerless to act until the constitution has been revised.
Then we had the spectacle of the Prime Minister returning to his own constituency and discussing this question with his constituents, but apparently in a different capacity. It must have been in a different capacity because the Prime Minister took a very different line. He is reported as having said this: practically all federal Liberals then said-
This is two years ago.
they did not want to start becoming involved in constitutional questions. There were more urgent problems housing, integration, poverty,-"and the constitution was pretty low in order of priorities."
"I was saying it, and the Liberal party in Ottawa was saying it"-
Said the Prime Minister. So you have the situation where in his own constituency the Prime Minister says that housing, integration and poverty are far higher in the scale of priority than reform of the constitution. Yet in this house the Prime Minister says that nothing effective can be done with regard to housing until the constitution is reformed. Just how cynical can a government get?
lYe have also had a phoney NATO review. In this regard the government has been facing in both directions. We now see the Prime Minister trying to look in both directions at once on the question of the constitution When we place the poor Minister of Transport in the context of the remarks made by the Prime Minister, there is certainly very little ground for the Minister of Transport to stand on.
Clearly the Prime Minister is a reluctant reformer of the constitution. He indicates in his speech that his hand has been forced by
Business of Supply
members of the opposition. Yet the other day in this house he said that, without substantial constitutional change, both his government and other governments in this country were virtually powerless to act in regard to housing.
Put the two positions side by side and the conclusion is inescapable. The Prime Minister believes that the government is powerless to act because of the constitution. Yet he did not seek constitutional change. Any government which, through its Prime Minister, simultaneously tries to adopt two positions is patently insincere when it tries to persuade the country that it is genuinely concerned about the urgency of the housing problem in this country. For that reason alone the minister's image as a reformer lacks credibility. The Prime Minister himself considers the Minister of Transport powerless under the existing constitution to carry out certain reforms. From what the Prime Minister said it is clear that there is no real will within the government to bring about constitutional change.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I do not accept the position that governments in this country are powerless to deal effectively with problems of housing, pollution, and so on. There are ways in which the provincial and federal governments may cooperate, but the Minister of Transport did not chose to follow the path of co-operation. He did not, as he ought to have, involve the provinces in the establishment and work of the task force. From the beginning he did not follow the road of co-operation. In short, once again this government is up to its old tricks, like the one performed with medicare where the government produced a program and asked the provinces to take it over.
Clearly, the Minister of Transport was operating in an area of divided jurisdiction. Nevertheless, he acted from the beginning in this matter without taking cognizance of the proper role of the provinces in solving the housing problem. It would have been much wiser to involve the provinces. They could have enlightened the task force considerably about certain aspects of the problem, and there would have been a better measure of real co-operation in the solution of our housing problem. The minister concerned turned his back on the provinces, and I will not be surprised if he achieves nothing substantial in the solution of the housing problem.
The Prime Minister thinks that little can be done under the present constitution; he persists in making inflammatory statements

March 4, 1969
Business of Supply
which do little to enhance federal-provincial co-operation. Because of the Prime Minister's views, the position of the Minister of Transport lacks credibility.
As I have said, the Minister of Transport was not prepared to co-operate with the provinces. But I have another reason for saying that his position lacks credibility. Under his direction the task force, among other things, recommended that in certain instances the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials ought to be abolished.. Clearly, that recommendation emanated from the minister; equally clearly, the Minister of Finance, who also has responsibility in this field, has no intention of going along with this recommendation. It was bad enough when the Postmaster General poked his nose into the affairs of the Departments of External Affairs and National Defence and expressed views in public contrary to those known to be held by the government. Whether he did so to hide the chaos in his own department or because someone had asked him to undermine the position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs is beside the point. But in the housing field two ministers who are jointly responsible, in a manner of speaking, are in open conflict and are apparently recommending different policies.
I ask, Mr. Chairman, what goes on in this government? How often will the government look both ways at once? How often will it wear two faces at the same time? We have seen it doing that on the NATO question, on constitutional questions, and we are now seeing it with regard to the 11 per cent sales tax. The minister's present position is patently phony. If the government does not act on the recommendation of his task force that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials be abolished, will he resign as a minister of this government? Is he prepared to resign? If he is not prepared to resign, his position is patently phony and insincere.

We want the minister to behave as he ought to behave, to have the courage of his convictions and to stand behind the public positions he takes. It is time integrity was restored in matters of public behaviour and it is time ministers stuck to their principles.

Last night the minister advanced an argument regarding removal of the ceiling on N.H.A. loans and strengthened our conviction that he cannot be believed. Since coming to Ottawa I have never heard anything more absurd than the position the minister advanced last evening. He argued that removing the ceiling would ensure a steady flow of mortgage funds, and the inference I drew was that interest rates would climb above the present ceiling. Then in the same breath he argued that this action would reduce mortgage interest rates. Well, he cannot have it both ways. I only hope that no one in the government will pay the slightest attention to that recommendation which can only send up interest rates on mortgages when funds are already in short supply. Although the minister explained his report last night, his position lacks credibility. We hope that at least one of his recommendations will not be adopted by the government. Of course, we d;d not really need to hear the minister explain what his task force was recommending. Through carefully contrived leaks or releases many of the recommendations of the task force had already been made public even before the report was tabled in the house.
We were told that the report constituted a revolutionary approach to the housing problems of Canada. I ask, what was revolutionary about it?

Many of them I advocated, but when I advocated them my hon. friends opposite said they were socialistic. They scorned those ideas.

I have to believe these statements, Mr. Chairman, because I would think any minister would be too ashamed to admit to them unless they were true. The minister stated that the federal government has obviously been involved in housing for many years in this country. He said that there had been no research done to determine the effect of supply in relation to rents. There had been no research done to see what the effects were of a 3 per cent or 5 per cent vacancy rate in a city. I find this almost impossible to believe even for this government, Mr. Chairman. I would not have believed it if anybody else had said it, but when the minister responsible said it I had to accept it. It really makes me wonder whether the government is capable of properly managing anything in connection with housing.
The minister made an amazing statement regarding public housing. He said it was the first time he had been exposed to the views of tenants. I daresay that is true although some of the rest of us have been. Is it credible? It must be, but it is hard to believe that a Crown agency involved in assisting in the construction of public housing and encouraging municipalities to engage in public housing would not follow up on its projects to determine the attitude of the tenants in such public housing. Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman, any competent government putting a good deal of money into public housing and then not taking the trouble to determine whether these were good healthy surroundings for the tenants?
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I cannot believe that the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are not fully informed on this matter. Here I must believe it was the minister who was ignorant. I cannot believe that the officials who are putting all this money into these public housing plans had not taken the trouble to inform themselves as to what satisfaction these projects were giving to the people living in them. I cannot take the minister seriously on that one.
Where do we stand with regard to these projects in the future? The minister purported to be very specific and definite. He suggested it was only where urban renewal

schemes involving business development were concerned that there would be postponements, but I defy anyone to go over what he said and determine what is the actual position now with regard to public housing projects. We are not a bit wiser today than we were before he spoke and, of course, before he spoke we were not a bit wiser than we were when he refused to answer questions in the house a few day ago. The minister's position is very obscure. When the minister stands up in the house and says there was only one year in which there was any real short-fall in the construction of housing, then that is about the end of it. I do not see how he could expect any of us to take him seriously after that statement.
We all agree that there is no simple solution to the housing problem. Presumably the government is going to continue to exercise the authority granted it by the people of Canada, and presumably it will hold office for the normal term.. I presume this will be the case and that the minister or somebody else will have the responsibility of moving forward with housing programs. Therefore it is important that the minister and the government restore their credibility in this field.
It is important that we have some clarification with regard to the constitution and the effect of the constitution on the minister's programs. Is it virtually impossible, as the Prime Minister suggested, for us to proceed with a housing program under the present constitution? If this is so, how does the Prime Minister explain that constitutional reform is low on the scale of priorities? I would like to hear the Prime Minister explain that to the house some time. I would like the government to take a credible position with regard to this matter. I would like the minister and the government to move to restore their relationships with the provinces.
Today we had another sign of the government going off half-cocked in connection with offshore mineral rights, violating undertakings given by previous prime ministers to engage in consultation with the provinces. This is exactly the way that the Minister of Transport is going about solving the housing problem which the Prime Minister says cannot be solved under the existing constitution.
I say, stop the farce with regard to the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. Stop exposing us to the spectacle of one minister urging its abolition and then the Minister of Finance pouring scorn on the idea. Let them

stop the pretence that they are doing anything to lower the cost of money to the homeowner. Stop the pretence that they are busy doing something by way of an anti-inflationary program. Let them provide some relief along the lines I have suggested, or along other lines, to those homeowners troubled with the fantastically high interest rates for which the government is primarily responsible.
At the moment the minister's position is completely incredible. I have gone over the reasons for this and through you, Mr. Chairman, I want to tell the committee that we are very concerned about the condition of housing in this country. We believe that the problem can be attacked. We do not share the view of the Prime Minister that the present state of the constitution makes an effective attack virtually impossible. If the government will improve its relations with the provinces, obviously an effective attack can be made.
There are some good ideas in the task force report. There have to be other ideas added to them. These ideas are being discussed. We in the Official Opposition will support and assist the minister in launching and carrying out an effective and comprehensive housing program but we want it to be credible, we want it to be sincere, we want it to be straightforward. We have had enough of these positions of duplicity.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened carefully to the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition. One thing that should be added to them is that in effect for the first time the federal government has focused its attention on the question of housing, which has provincial and municipal implications, and has produced a report on the problem which is perhaps the most comprehensive ever made on it in our history. In doing so the government has provided all those interested in searching for a solution with the opportunity to choose priorities and to decide on the kind of orientation we wish for a federal housing policy. In the past few years a large number of conferences on housing have been held and many speeches have been made. But never before has there been a study that has condensed in so comprehensive a manner all of the various aspects related to the issue, perhaps the most formidable and difficult issue facing any government in the western world, an issue that must be resolved.
Business of Supply
It might be very easy to resolve the housing problem under different economic conditions in other parts of the world, but in the western world with its free economy, with an explosion in population, in a country with such vast distances as Canada, with such diverse climatic conditions, with population increases continually taking place in some major urban centres and not in others, it is extremely difficult to produce a policy which will make everybody happy and will meet the needs in every corner of the country. On that score alone the Minister of Transport ought to be commended for having undertaken such an enormous task and for having produced in such a short time a document for us to debate and improve upon. I believe it is the beginning of a new trend wherein the federal government by virtue of other circumstances has found it necessary to focus its attention on municipal matters and on powers given to other levels of government, including the municipal level.
From examining the report everyone interested in the subject could perhaps arrive at different conclusions and different priorities with respect to the final policy which ought to emerge, and there are a few points I would like to submit in contributing to this debate as best I can.
The report in its declaration of principles says that the housing needs of most Canadians can and should be met through the private market. This is quite true so far as the production of housing is concerned in the form of new apartment buildings and new houses of a certain size. But the pattern in large urban centres, and I can only speak from experience of large urban centres, indicates that the private sector has not been in a position to produce public housing. Therefore the government, in its priorities and orientation, should include public housing. In doing so it could draw on and benefit from the studies which have already been completed and carried on over a number of years. It could draw on the experience of others.

When we speak of public housing we hear criticisms in respect of the shortage of certain social facilities such as day nurseries, recreational centres and the like. This is the very kind of thing that could improve the quality of future public housing projects. when it comes to public housing, that society derives from public housing social benefits in many different related and perhaps unrelated areas. Therefore this is a field of human endeavour which deserves a continuity of effort.
While dispersed acquisition of houses in any given community in respect of public housing might be very desirable from a social viewpoint, this policy will not add to the housing stock available. It will actually diminish the housing stock available from the private sector and therefore would have the effect of increasing the cost of the units available on the market. There is the suggestion, for instance, that perhaps loans should be made available as subsidies for the payment of rent. I would rather see a different objective. If loans are to be made available as subsidies I believe they should be made available not for rental purposes, because they would eventually end up in the pockets of the landlord in one form or another, but as loans toward the purchase of a housing unit.
It must also be emphasized that when we speak of housing programs and projects for the Indian, Eskimo and Metis people in many parts of Canada our attention should also be focused on the situation in the major urban areas of Canada where there is a large influx of immigrants. This situation will certainly require our attention because immigrants who will arrive in years to come will find difficulty in obtaining accommodation upon arrival.
Much has been said on the subject of urban renewal. In this regard I think the views expressed in the report are very useful for the purpose of focusing attention on what has been done so far and on the shortcomings in the techniques which have been adopted so far. I do not know that great benefit will be derived by the suspension of urban renewal schemes. I would rather that we continued our efforts and eliminated the feeling of uncertainty which has been created in some of our centres because of the suspension. Some of the projects which are awaiting approval are of a highly sophisticated nature and would meet the thinking, expectations and hopes of the task force even beyond their dreams. These projects have been produced by local groups with the co-operation of the local government and through a process of dialogue over a period of months and years of co-operation.
Therefore the question of urban renewal perhaps should be approached in the light of

experience. Perhaps it could be expanded in a way so that rather than doing it on a limited area basis of a few blocks or a square mile it could be done by approaching it as a renewal project for any given municipality. Thus it could be incorporated in the same way a municipality would incorporate a public works program. This concept should be the broadest possible within the confines of the municipality and should eliminate the atmosphere of uncertainty and discomfort that some urban renewal schemes have created in the past.
The question of loans and grants for the rehabilitation of existing housing is a very crucial one. It is a question of great importance in the older portions of our cities. I submit it is not possible to expect an elderly couple who live on a fixed income to receive a loan for the renewal of their house. It would perhaps be desirable to develop a system whereby rather than a loan a grant would be made available for the improvement of the property and this grant would then become an encumbrance on the title of the house. The repayment of the grant to the lending authority could be worked out on that basis. At present I believe it would be unrealistic to expect people to renew their homes on the basis of loans, particularly when they have a limited income.
There are several more points which I could discuss such as the question of individual rehabilitation which has taken place in some areas and the theory of the filtering down of housing. What is happening right now in large centres is that houses are no longer filtering down from one social stratum to another but are actually filtering up. Many people find it desirable to buy a home at a reasonable price on the market, improve it and then sell it on the market at a much higher price. So we are actually experiencing a reverse process which could be called filtering up.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened very attentively a while ago to the remarks of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) on the housing legislation and supplementary estimates we are asked to approve, in order to give better assistance in the housing field in Canada.
This housing legislation is of outstanding importance since it is of utmost concern and interest to thousands of Canadians calling for better dwelling and a housing program adapted to the average Canadian, not programs like those that are submitted to us, involving very high rates of interest supposedly to fight inflation.
The cost of money is going up all the time and the reason given for that is that we must fight inflation. On the other hand, the minister introduces a piece of legislation to increase housing credits, on the pretence that we need
Under the present housing act, Mr. Chairman, a Canadian worker who decides to buy a $15,000 home must now pay interest at a rate of 10 per cent. If it takes him 35 years to pay for his house, it will have cost him more than $60,000, including the interest, and excluding municipal and school taxes. This is, to me, an inflationary scheme in itself, for that $15,000 home will never be worth $60,000. Yet, that is the bill we are asked to pass.
Where are the Canadians who will be able to pay $175 or $200 a month for 35 years to own their home? Indeed-and the minister is aware of it

many small home owners who bought a house 5, 6 or 8 years ago now have to give them up, losing by doing so the savings they had accumulated over 10 or 15 years, because of the increase in school and municipal taxes, and the cost of rental or monthly payments.
For instance, is there an E. B. Eddy employee in Hull who can pay $200 a month for a $15,000 home? There is not and the minister knows it. Built-up areas are multiplying in the suburbs of Montreal, Toronto, and other large centres.
Yet, in Montreal, hundreds of houses are empty, because workers cannot hope to live in that type of housing. Even if $600,000,000 or even $1 billion were spent to build new housing units, if the terms and conditions are not within the reach of the Canadian buyer, people will certainly not be helped towards better housing.
Thousands of families are still living in Montreal slums; they cannot hope to move to a more comfortable and decent home, and pay $175 or $200 a month.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The minister and the government know this is impossible, but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) goes on repeating across Canada that money does not grow on trees and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) also agrees with this. There is a lack of money and it costs too much.
A while ago, the Leader of the Opposition was saying that the cost of money should be reduced. How would he go about it? We do not know because he is not telling. What would he do if he were the present minister or heading the present government? We do not know. We know ourselves that interest rates are too high and that is why we have been fighting in this house since 1962. I was doing so way

back in 1946-23 years ago-and I used to tell the government: Why not finance those projects of national importance through interest-free loans by the Bank of Canada as this is being done for India, Africa, South America, China and other countries throughout the world? Why not assist Canadians in the same way through the services of this financial institution which belongs to all Canadians, that is the Bank of Canada? On the contrary, this control is left in the hands of Canadian bankers who tell the Bank of Canada what to do. This institution does not exert any authority over the chartered banks of which it is the servant instead of exercising its own sovereign powers as a servant of the people and abiding by the decisions of the Parliament of Canada. It is merely the toy of outside financial interests which are dictating their own terms to the government.
The government is now willing to guarantee loans. To whom? To the companies which, in turn, will lend at an interest rate of 10 or 12 per cent, if not 15 or 20 per cent. That is what is being done by the insurance companies 'and by the banks. Insurance companies, incidentally, do not give any credit. Money does not grow in their case but, on the other hand, it grows in banks. This is where it is born through the law which allows bankers to multiply by 14 every central government bond. Would it be more difficult for the central government to make the multiplication by 14 itself instead of entrusting with this task some individuals who, in turn, lend to the government at outrageous interest rates? It is in order to protect those financial bloodsuckers that the government brings in such laws. One has not even the right to rise in order to protest against these rights granted to financiers.
Mr. Chairman, the Creditistes are the only ones who have the courage to object to this shameful exploitation of the Canadian nation and of the Canadian government. Money does not grow on trees. No. It grows in banks. The insurance companies borrow from banks and, in most cases, it is they that grant loans to people who need a home or want to develop resources and so on.
The banks are the masters because they are the greatest power in Canada. Without their permission, nobody has the right to breathe. It is as clear as that. The trust companies, the finance companies and the insurance companies constitute, as it were, the offspring of the banks. One hears people criticize the insurance companies, the trust companies and [Mr. Caouette.l
others by saying: let us get rid of these companies. Let us kill the children and let the mother live. I think it is the best way to insure that she will have other children in a few years. The only way to prevent the exploitation of the Canadian people is to take away from the banks the power to encourage the creation of trust companies.
Mr. Chairman, the housing problem does not concern Ottawa only. Besides, the minister, the Prime Minister and the government admit it. It concerns also the provinces, the municipalities and the citizens. A while ago I heard a Liberal member say that, in the future, the central government would have to reach a compromise directly with the authorities of the great cities. Solving the problems of the provinces would be easier, in my opinion, for the provincial authorities than for the federal government because those problems are closer to the former than to the latter, and when the provinces insist on having more say in the field of housing, I believe they are right.
I do not think there is any need to amend the constitution for the sake of giving the provinces a larger measure of responsibility in the field of housing. I bet the Premier of Quebec has seen the slums of that province more often than the Minister of Transport under whose jurisdiction comes the question of housing. I am pretty sure that the provincial authorities are more aware of the situation in Montreal than the federal minister, the Prime Minister or the central government. It is agreed that, under the constitution, it is a field directly pertaining to the federal authority. It is in fact, its very own field: I am referring to the matter of financing. The question of money and credit is Ottawa's business and not that of the provinces. That is why the representatives of the provinces come to Ottawa and ask the minister or the government: Give us the financial means, for, at the moment, all we have is the responsibility.
Such is the problem facing the government in every field, specially in housing.
So the provinces come to Ottawa, saying: Give us the funds. Ottawa answers: We do not have any.. Money does not grow on trees. Such is the kind of answer given by the Prime Minister. Then where does money come from? The Prime Minister does not know. He knows, but he does not have the right to tell. As for me, I know it and I have the right to tell. And I do. Whether you like it or not, the truth is there and I say it bluntly.

Mr. Chairman, financial means should be made available to the provinces thus enabling them to enact a law on housing to provide every Canadian with the means of buying a decent home but not at the present rates of interest. The present situation should not be allowed to last or to deteriorate for it is worse than it was five years ago, as far as housing is concerned. In fact, to live in a small family home costs a lot more today than it did five or six years ago.
Assistance has just been granted to Montreal-and that has nothing to do with housing. The Minister of Transport is 'aware of it. It has to do with the granting of rather important sums of money, interest free, to make up Expo's deficit. We begin to understand that to pay off deficits, we will have to resort to a procedure advocated by the Creditistes for the past 30 years. I am referring to interest free financing. In order to help out Expo in Montreal, the central government undertakes now to back it up with $8 million under an agreement with the province and the municipality, and without interest. It is a form of assistance and not a gift. It is a loan that the City of Montreal will have to pay back but without interest.
Why? Because it is a deficit incurred by Expo. I do not blame the government for granting an interest-free loan to the City of Montreal, on the contrary I congratulate it for that. It should do the same for the municipalities which are short of money.
There are not only municipal deficits; there are 'also provincial deficits, school deficits, personal deficits. People have gone into debt for 5, 10, 15 and even 35 years to buy a house. I said earlier that very few people will become homeowners if purchasing plans of 25, 30 and 35 years are established. If a Canadian gets a house when he is 35 or 40, and pays for it little by little that is by instalments spread over a long period, he will be 70 or 75 before he is through paying for it. Who will live until 75 with an old age pension of $107 a month? Who will still own his house at that time?
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, we will probably leave that to our children, thus mortgaging the future of our children and that of their own children. The present Minister of Transport or myself will not be around then, but the inheritors of our debts will. We are the ones who will have voted those debts in this house.

Mr. Chairman, housing is a national matter of which both Ottawa and the provinces are responsible. I repeat that the provinces have all they need at their disposal to proceed with housing projects for the materials and the workers are available. Moreover, there are
200,000	unemployed in the province of Quebec alone, which is amazing in 1969, when there is so much to do. There are 80,000 unemployed in the city of Montreal alone. What a marvelous situation!
Why are there unemployed in the province of Quebec and elsewhere in Canada? Would it be because there are no more resources to develop, no more houses and no more highways to build, nothing more to undertake. Certainly not, Mr. Chairman. It is because money does not grow on trees because trees are not productive at the present time. There are no developments, because of procrastination, introduction of legislations, but all that does nothing to improve the economic situation in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, the central government ought to provide banks with financial means by allowing them to make use of the Bank of Canada; then you will see houses being built up for families, rather than families being planned according to houses as proposed by the C.M.H.C. For families with eight or ten children, they build small four room houses. Can you imagine 12 people crowded into four rooms. This does not make any sense. However, that is what the national housing act provides.
But one never hears about houses being built for large families, because they would be much too expensive. It is not on account of a shortage of building materials, manpower or land, but because the cost of money is too high; the money problem is the only problem they refuse to correct, to deal with. Money does not grow on trees. We take it in the pockets of Canadians. But where does it come from? Where does it grow? The government knows it, but it does not have the right to tell us.
Mr. Chairman, we maintain that a responsible and sovereign government should see to it to make financially possible what is physically feasible and desirable. On the other hand, the governments, whether Progressive Conservative or Liberal, have not taken their responsibilities, I think, in a number of fields, specially in the economic field. They have been satisfied with statements of principles, with talk about their love for the Canadian people, our natural inexhaustible resources,

the vastness of our country so dear to everyone. Even in 1935, the then Prime Minister, Mr. William Lyon Mackenzie King, made a statement that I always keep in my pocket, because I always fall back on it and find it of much value. Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation.

Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation.

Mr. Chairman, the same problem is still with us in 1969. In 1931, 38 years ago, Pope Pius XI said: "Those in control of money and credit are the masters of us all and nobody is allowed to breathe without their permission". This is just as true nowadays as it was then.

We also know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) seems much concerned about it, since he said recently, in Vancouver I believe, that he would be willing to leave his present position to head a department of housing if it were established by the government.
Considering the importance of the Department of Transport, I wonder if it would be in the best interests of the Canadian people to entrust the minister with new responsibilities and ask him to deal with the housing problem. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should relieve the Minister of Transport and entrust someone else, a Minister without Portfolio for example, with a matter as important as housing. Of course if the Minister of Transport would rather look after housing, he could leave the Department of Transport and become solely responsible for that important and essential matter which we call the housing policy.
I do not question the good intentions nor the good will of the minister. Indeed, he has established the so-called task force, a study group to consider the various aspects of the housing problem in Canada. I have studied that report like all other hon. members but I find in it very few practical solutions. It is obvious that excellent suggestions are made, but they are long-term suggestions which could not immediately solve the very important housing problem.
The main improvement has been an extension of the refund period of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. And, as many hon. members have repeated it in this house, Mr. Chairman, that measure does not in any way settle the matter.
Yesterday, replying to an opposition member who was criticizing the organization of the task force which has drafted the report we are studying, the minister said that he
Business of Supply
had chosen the finest authorities in the field to advise him.
I take the minister to task because if the federal government wants to take the responsibility of housing it should consult the provinces before proceeding with the detailed study of that very important problem since, as has been said by many hon. members, housing falls in the legal category of property and civil rights and hence under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. So, I wonder-perhaps the minister will give me an answer later on-if he intends to raise another constitutional conflict with the provinces. I think he should have included in this task force some provincial representatives who could, in the light of their government's information, provide the minister with most valuable data on housing.
A member said earlier that the provinces and the municipalities are much closer to the people than the federal government, which is true. It is also the responsibility of the provinces to discuss with the municipalities the problems of housing, property rights, and civil rights. So I do not see how the minister can, constitutionally speaking, discuss directly with the municipalities of the country without doing so through the provinces. Besides, the minister knows that in constitutional matters, he has no authority over municipalities. By insisting on going forward with a housing policy without consulting the provinces, I wonder if the minister is not about to create another constitutional crisis between the provinces and the federal government? The minister is well aware of that since, at the recent conference of representatives of municipalities and provinces held in Toronto, which he attended, he was severely warned, especially by the province of Quebec, not to elaborate detailed policies without consulting the provinces, and especially Quebec, because that is a field that falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
Mr. Chairman, I say that the minister's behaviour is strange. I do not blame him for attempting to help Canadians, for bringing forward policies likely to solve the housing problem in some sectors. The minister may want to point out that under the constitution, the federal government must look after the welfare of all Canadians and the minister would be right. But until the Canadian constitution is amended, neither he nor the federal government have the right to interfere directly in a jurisdiction that belongs exclusively to the provinces.

March 4. 1969
Business of Supply
In fact, the first step the minister should take would be to invite the provinces to a conference on the housing problem. Conferences have already been held in 1965 and 1966, and the minister will remember-even if he was not the minister responsible for housing then-that the provinces had raised objections with regard to the constitutionality of the exclusive control of housing by the federal government, wondering whether that problem did not lie exclusively within the provincial jurisdiction. We remember that at that time, the conference had dealt with one definite point.
I am surprised today that the government and the minister are now asking us to vote supplementary estimates in an effort to solve the housing problem. I am wondering whether in view of the differences of opinion expressed by some provinces in this constitutional field, the minister should not rather begin by calling together the provinces in order to discuss the problem with them and to work out plans which might solve housing problems in Canada.
The minister knows that several provinces, including Quebec, already have a housing corporation. Everything must be done to avoid duplication, in which case the same service to be available both at the federal and at the provincial levels of government. This is why provinces are complaining; they need fiscal resources in order to establish their own housing corporation.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Presently, the Quebec housing corporation is borrowing from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at an interest rate unknown to me, but which is below the rate approved by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). Then, the Quebec housing corporation lends money to Quebecers so they can build houses. So, Mr. Chairman, we have, sharing the same field, the Quebec housing corporation and Ottawa's Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which are competing on the same market. In my view, we should settle this once for all. However, I submit that even if the minister established committees made up of experts the main problem would still remain, we still would have to call together the provinces with a view to define responsibilities at each level of government and to draw up a comprehensive program which could help all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to congratulate the minister on his good will, when he expressed

his intention to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials.
It is known that since 1965 when this tax was imposed, and even before that, we, of the Progressive Conservative party and of the official opposition, have made representations to the Minister of Finance suggesting that this tax would only slow up the development of this important sector, housing. If the minister considers not only the urban centres-which we hear so much about in the house-but also rural areas like the one I represent, he will realize that there are also in the latter housing problems.
In my home town, for instance with a population of 6,000 inhabitants, some people are unable to find an apartment to rent. There are also people who live in dilapidated houses, when they might have enough capital to build their own house. But how can they do it, when they must pay first of all an 11 per cent tax on building materials, which is an inflationary measure?
When the minister made a statement suggesting that he was in favour of removing the 11 per cent tax, he was right. And I think he should try to convince the Minister of Finance as well as his colleagues, to do so because it is a matter requiring first priority.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to participate in this debate because I feel we have not paid enough attention to low-income Canadians in rural areas and in the cities. The task force did not pay enough attention to them, and for that reason I wish to make a few comments.
There is nothing new about our present housing crisis. There has always been a housing crisis for Canadians with low incomes or no incomes. As we know, the housing shortage has grown and now affects the middle-income groups. The government set up the task force because the shortage has become a political issue. Many votes are to be gained among middle-income Canadians. Our middle-income groups became concerned about the crisis and finally they wanted answers. They realized they could no longer have adequate and decent housing, and for that reason we are engaged in the present debate. I do not say the task force ought to have visited every little village in Canada, but it did not pay too much attention to our rural population mainly, I suspect, because about 75 per cent of our people live in urban centres.
What does this government propose to do for our low-income families? To qualify for a mortgage loan one's income must be in excess of $8,000. I understand. I do not know how many of the recommendations of the task force will be adopted, but I wish to ask this question. Does the minister intend to make housing available to families with incomes of $5,000 a year? It would be good if we could achieve that. But what of families with incomes of less than $5,000 a year? Many such families exist in our cities and rural areas. Many of our simple, hard-working citizens earn between $50 and $75 a week. They are honest and deserve homes. But, from my reading of the task force report, no provision is made for them.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
A news release of the Canadian Conference on Housing quotes Dr. Albert Rose, Proffessor

March 4, 1969
Business of Supply
at the University of Toronto School of Social Work, as follows:
The most important change that could be made in our national housing policy would be a formal declaration that the federal and provincial governments intended, during the balance of this century, to discriminate in favour of families and individuals at the bottom half of the income distribution.
The news release continues:
This group he says includes Canadian Indians and members of other minority groups; the elderly and the not so elderly who are single, widowed, or otherwise alone in society; families headed by women with dependent children; families of chronically ill male heads, and so on.
This is quite true. In a town in my own constituency, out of a total of 2,695 wage earners 965 heads of families earn $2,000 or less per annum. This is typical in rural Canada and in many instances in urban Canada. Many Canadians fall into this category. Leaving aside for a moment wage earners in the low salary bracket and dealing with the $3,000 to $5,000 a year group, 60 per cent or two-thirds of our wage earners are in this group. The government is attempting to provide housing only for those earning in excess of $5,000 a year.
There are many in Nova Scotia earning $250, $300 and $400 a month, and I believe the same holds true all across Canada. They are perfectly honest hard-working citizens, but they cannot afford a home. The only way these people in my area are able to have a home is if their father owns a small farm and provides them with the land, lumber and help. These people usually know how to ham die a hammer and saw and can help in this way. Many tradesmen are not able to borrow in order to build a home. In urban areas it is almost impossible for someone earning $250 or $300 a month to purchase a home with the cost of living as high as it is. The government is offering nothing to families where the head of the family earns less than $5,000.
I have nothing against raising the mortgage ceiling from $18,000 to $35,000, but what does it do? It provides those who can already obtain a loan or a home with better housing. There is nothing wrong with that, but it does not provide adequate housing for those in the lower income bracket. These people cannot afford high interest rates of 9 per cent on the first mortgage and possibly 15 per cent on a second mortgage. This government is not interested in solving the housing crisis but simply in creating the impression that they are gods in this field. They really do not intend to do much to solve the problem. It

has become a political issue. The government is trying to satisfy the middle-class people and provide better housing for those who can already afford a home.
Many good suggestions have been made by the task force. The leader of the Liberal party in Nova Scotia last night stated that Nova Scotia has the greatest housing crisis in the country. I hope he will make representations to the federal government. If the government is not interested in the low-income groups or cannot solve the housing crisis in those groups, then at least the task force should have recommended ways and means for people with low incomes to raise their standard of living. Possibly they should have recommended steps to be taken by the new Department of Regional Economic Development in order to raise the standard of living for these families so they would qualify for loans under the act.
The members of the Progressive Conservative party, and I am sure all hon. members, are interested in seeing that all Canadian families are provided with adequate and decent housing.

If I may deal with a rather narrow aspect of the housing subject, it seems quite clear that price increases over the past five years have been a major factor in making the housing problem in Canada more critical. I would like to deal with the problem of price and more particularly to refer to the "gold" paper on policies for price stability issued by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in December of last year.
March 4, 1969

[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
In the foreword to that document the minister suggested that the paper might serve as a basis for further consultation with interested economic groups. But surely any policy to maintain price stability must look to having an important impact on housing. I think that there may be the lingering thought in the minds of some people, certainly in my constituency, that the idea of establishing a prices and incomes board on a voluntary basis might be construed as simply another blatant pitch for more empire building and that indeed it would not go very far toward meeting the kind of problems that the report discusses.
The paper issued by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs describes the Prices and Incomes Commission and what it might do in these terms:
It will be charged with the responsibility for conducting studies of incomes and price developments in Canada, and for producing regular reports on its findings. The purpose of the commission will be to discover the facts, analyse the causes, processes and consequences of inflation, and to inform both the public and the government on how price stability may be achieved. It will not play the role of policeman. It will not intervene in the particular price and income decisions of individual persons, business firms, or trade unions. It will be empowered, however, to undertake research and inquiries and issue periodic public reports on current trends and prospects for prices, costs, incomes and productivity for the economy as a whole; to make similar studies and reports on various broad sectors and industries; and to engage in related investigations of other broad issues which may have a bearing on cost and price movements . .. To carry out this broad and difficult role, the commission will be given adequate powers of inquiry. It will be provided with the necessary budget and an expert staff. It will also be authorized to engage consultants, and to arrange for the conduct of research by the universities and other bodies as it finds appropriate.
In its preamble the document explains the problems of price stability in its efforts to justify the creation of the commission, and it says:
The conclusion drawn by the government of Canada from our recent experience is that the present policy tools are not sufficient to resolve the very real conflict that exists at the present time between the objectives of maintaining high level employment and restoring the price stability that is necessary for sustained economic growth.
It may be that by applying the conventional monetary and fiscal levers with sufficient force, the inflation of the past three years could have been brought to a halt. But the immediate cost in terms of the level of unemployment and output foregone would certainly have been high.
Business of Supply
I would like to remind the committee, if it be necessary, that the last federal surplus was in 1956. Evidently the fiscal levers that have been discussed here have been largely untried. According to received economic theory, a budget which is neither stimulating nor restraining is a surplus budget since the expenditure multiplier is higher than the tax multiplier. In the last several years, moreover, the money supply has been expanded at an abnormally high rate.
In order to receive exemptions from certain United States measures to halt the gold drain, Canada was committed not to hold more than a maximum number of U.S. dollars. In order to stay below this ceiling, and to keep the exchange rate between Canadian and American dollars fixed, it was necessary to expand the domestic money supply. If Canada were to revert to a floating exchange rate, monetary policy would again become available as a tool for fighting inflation, and I am suggesting, Mr. Chairman, that this is one of the points which has a very direct bearing on housing and the money that is available for housing purposes. In so far as conventional monetary and fiscal levers are concerned, it might be suggested that if we have not tried them we should not spend too much time knocking them.
As a justification for some sort of incomes policy the O.E.C.D. Economic Survey of Canada was cited. In this survey, published in 1968, the O.E.C.D. concluded its analysis of Canada's recent cost and price problems with the following words:
Canada's price-wage performance in full employment conditions suggests that there is need for some sort of an income policy. A number of other O.E.C.D. countries have been active in this field in the last few years. No country can point to any spectacular success in controlling the rise in incomes this way. This perhaps is not surprising, given the nature of the problems involved progress could hardly be expected to be very rapid. There are indications, however, that income policy in some countries is beginning to play a useful role . . . The decentralized character of the Canadian economy may render the evolution of an incomes policy more difficult than in many European countries, but this may not be a reason for dispensing altogether with efforts in this direction.
It is interesting that two pages later a table showing rises in the consumer price indices of various O.E.C.D. countries reveals that inflation has been less severe in Canada than in any other country except the United States of America, and substantially lower than any O.E.C.D. country which has an incomes policy. Indeed, one can only reiterate, "No country can point to spectacular success in controlling the rise in incomes this way."

March 4, 1969
Business of Supply
The causes of rising prices are again discussed in this report and the question is posed:
What are the underlying reasons for our recent unsatisfactory price behavior? .. . We lack adequate statistical data and sufficient empirical research in the area of price and income determination in Canada. Thus we are confronted today with explanations that are contradictory and differ with the approach in the particular economic interests of those undertaking the analysis or offering their wage prescriptions-
The document expounds on reasons for changes in relative price, unused resources and so forth, and then talks about time lags in implementing monetary and fiscal policy. No mention is made of the time lag inherent in investigations by a prices and incomes commission into specific price and income changes and the introduction of remedies. Indeed, no indication is given in the whole document about what sorts of remedies might be appropriate to deal with any problems investigated by the commission.
The uncertainties as to how close to capacity the economy can operate without creating serious demand and inflationary pressures are mentioned. Bottleneck problems are also described, but again it is not made clear why these obstacles to the success of fiscal and monetary policy should be less formidable as obstacles to an incomes policy.
One question the document does not answer is: If resources are not to be allocated by a price mechanism, what other mechanism is to take its place? This question is relevant regardless of whether prices are kept down by regulation or through voluntary restraint.
The position of labour is an interesting one in this matter, and I quote from a comment contained in a document, "Labour Costs in Canada", issued by the Canadian Labour Congress:
Organized labour would resist any incomes policy which, either by design or interpretation, placed heavy responsibilities on labour for exercising wage restraints while allowing other forms of income to find their own level. On the other hand, labour would certainly give consideration to, and be prepared to discuss with other groups, an incomes policy or set of guidelines which took the returns of all factors of production into consideration.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
As I read this statement it seems that it simply says that if we are prepared to accept price and income control along with profit control and, indeed, a general control of business, we may expect to carry organized labour along with the concept of an income and prices control board. It seems to me this

is hardly the road we ought to follow in meeting the problem of price increases, particularly when we examine the contribution a financial policy might make toward an alleviation of the housing problem.
In the housing report many commendable suggestions respecting methods and organization are made, but I have the uncomfortable feeling that in the face of a 9 per cent to 10 per cent effective interest rate on mortgage funds a lot of these suggestions must assume a relatively unimportant place. The idea of extending the effective term of a mortgage loan to 40 years does not seem to be one that really gets at the basic issue, although it is of some immediate practical assistance. If we cannot get the cost of money down, then it seems that a housing crisis will persist unless there is a substantial increase in incomes or, alternatively, unless we are prepared to create a special financial market for housing.
I do not see that it is possible to contemplate the kind of increase in incomes that is necessary, nor do I see the possibility of creating an effective money market for housing funds that is insulated from the general trend of interest and prices. Certainly I think it is quite clear that the creation of types of voluntary activity such as envisaged by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in the prices and income board is not likely to provide a solution. On the other hand, an effective reduction in interest rates can in my submission only come about as a result of a monetary and fiscal policy that explicitly recognizes the effect that massive increases in the supply of money, under what has been generally called an easy money policy, have had on interest rates.
If we are to avoid a continuing crisis not only in housing finance but in the financing of any small enterprise, I think it is absolutely essential that our efforts be directed and devoted to bringing the effective rate of interest down through a controlled fiscal and monetary policy. I do not believe this in any sense represents a solution to the housing problem but I would remind you, Mr. Chairman, that typically the rate of housing development has moved inversely with the rate of interest and that the supply of money has not been particularly large during times when the interest rate has been high. In other words, I think there is some historic evidence to support the proposition that you can get adequate flows of capital into the housing market in the face of relatively modest interest rates. I therefore commend that section of the housing task force report that deals with finances
March 4, 1969

as being an important section. I would also suggest that a general review of our fiscal policy, having in mind the particular problems of housing, would be most appropriate and I would hope it would be done at an early date.
