speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hundreds of thousands of people in this country are living in totally inadequate housing accommodation. I am being very conservative when I say there are hundreds of thousands of people in every city in Canada, in the rural areas and in the mining communities, as well as Indians and Metis, who are living in inadequate housing accommodation. Probably a million or more people who are either purchasing homes or renting accommodation are paying substantially more than they can afford to spend on housing. They do so simply because no other accommodation is available at prices they can afford. So it did not take a task force to tell the people of Canada or the members of parliament that we face a housing crisis.
We have had studies at the national level by government departments. We have had studies at the national level carried on by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We have had studies at the provincial level by provincial governments, and we have had studies at the municipal level which have been carried on by the municipalities or by corporations established by the municipalities. If we had $1 for every study which has been carried out I am sure we would have sufficient funds to build a substantial number of the houses which are needed to meet the needs of the Canadian people. Therefore it made no sense to me when it was announced that a task force would be established to study housing needs in this country. Now that we have the report of the task force I am

March 4, 1969
Business of Supply
more than ever convinced that nothing useful can or will be obtained as a result of this study.
e (5:10 p.m.)
Before I go into what I think were the major faults of the task force I want to deal with some statements made yesterday by the minister. I am sure those statements satisfied no one but the minister and possibly the reporter for the C.B.C. who obviously has his housing problem solved. He did not see anything of value in what was said by members of the opposition.
The minister said there will be enough houses built in the coming year. He is confident as a result of discussions that there will be sufficient money available to provide the necessary financing. He went on to suggest that the freeing of interest rates on mortgages under government authorization, which took place some time ago, will sufficiently improve the housing situation to satisfy the needs of the low-income groups. The minister also suggested that we would meet the required 200,000 housing units this year. I suggest that this target is much too low, and that the interest rate of 9 per cent or higher will have the effect of freezing out more than 90 per cent of those people who wish to purchase homes.
The minister is not in his seat at this time but I hope he will pay attention to what I have to say as well as to the speeches by the hon. member for Greenwood and the Liberal member for Davenport. He pointed out the tremendous problems which exist in Toronto in respect of those people in the $5,000 to $6,000 income bracket who wish to obtain housing. Nothing the government has done up to now has had any effect on this situation, and nothing that the task force has recommended will have any effect.
Let me make a few remarks about the task force and its report. The minister said last night that its recommendations were unanimous. He took that as an indication of approval of the policies he recommended. Of course the recommendations of the task force were unanimous; the minister picked the members of that task force. He got a kangaroo court to act as jury and hangman. I have a great deal of respect for Mr. Campeau. He is an extremely successful builder, but he builds offices and buildings which he rents to the federal government and its departments at very high rents. He also builds houses and apartment buildings. I had the fortune or misfortune to live in one of Mr. Campeau's
[Mr. Orlikow.l
buildings for four years. It was a very good apartment building and I have no complaints about it. The bulk of the people in Ottawa and other cities who rent space in this kind of project find living simply impossible because they cannot afford the rents.
We have heard from that esteemed lady from Nova Scotia whose practical suggestion to the people living in public housing projects in the city of Toronto was that even those without children found it impossible to save money. I suppose they represent the people in the $5,000 to $6,000 income bracket. She suggested that they do without telephones as a means of saving money. In 100 years by saving $5 or $6 per month they might accumulate enough money to put a down payment on their own homes. That is the kind of people the minister put on the task force. Yet he now wonders why he received the kind of report he did.
There was not one single representative of labour or of co-operatives on that force. Dr. Laidlaw, the former secretary of the Co-operative Union of Canada, has had long experience in the field of housing in Canada, particularly housing for low income groups. He was not called upon for his advice or experience. There was not a single representative on the task force of the people who live in public housing projects already built. The minister wonders why we are dissatisfied with the report of the task force and its recommendations in respect of public housing.
The minister says it is his hope and intention that everybody in Canada will in the near future have the ability to obtain the kind of housing they want. What kind of a choice do the tens of thousands of people have who are receiving incomes of $3,000 or less? What kind of a choice do those people have who are living on welfare? What kind of choice do those thousands of people have who are separated from a husband or wife? Let me remind the minister that these people are trying to raise children. What choice do they have in respect of housing?
I suggest we have ignored those in the low income brackets who live in public housing projects. We have ignored also those people who would like to live in housing projects. The hon. member for Davenport mentioned that between 14,000 and 16,000 people in the city of Toronto have applied for public housing. What are we doing for them? We are ignoring them.
March 4, 1969

Michael Wheeler, an expert in the field of housing, in a speech he made to the annual conference of mayors and municipalities in 1967, pointed out that in the period from 1964 to 1966 some 84 per cent of the money the federal government spent on homes went to people in the middle and upper income brackets.
An expert in the field of public housing in Toronto once referred to this government practice as socialism for the rich. Only 6 per cent of federal government money is directed to housing for those people in the low income brackets. This is socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor. That is the type of housing program we have. We have ignored the needs of the people in the lower income brackets.
Now for the first time we have received a government document issued under the auspices of a minister of the Crown which in fact pours ridicule and scorn on the efforts we have made in the field of public housing. This document recommends that we stop even the miserably small effort that we have been making in this regard. Let me refer the Minister without Portfolio who comes from my own city to page 55 of the report of the task force. It states in part, as a recommendation of the task force:
The task force therefore recommends:
The federal government initiate a thorough research program into the economic, social and psychological issues of public housing. Until such a study is completed and assessed, no new large projects should be undertaken.
What has happened is that all federal housing projects have been suspended as of now until some time in the future. The minister has talked about the fact that the task force went out to interview people living in public housing projects and heard nothing but complaints. In case the minister does not know, let me tell him that if he talks to anybody living in public housing he will hear nothing but complaints. I can tell Mr. Campeau that I heard a great many complaints when I was living in his project, and it was a high-rise apartment, not a public housing project.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
One question which the minister and the task force should have asked the people living in public housing projects they obviously did not ask. It is a very simple question. They should have asked the people living in public housing projects: How do these accommodations compare with those in which you lived before? We have in my constituency a large
Business of Supply
housing project, the Burrows Keewatin project. I have criticisms of that project, but I tell the Minister of Transport, and I think the Minister without Portfolio knows this, that the accommodations there are 1,000 per cent better than the slums from which those people came.
A new housing project has just been opened in a corner of the constituency represented by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. There is a good deal wrong with it. It has walls around it six feet high. I do not know why. This makes it look like a prison. I do not like that. But I tell the Minister of Transport that this accommodation is infinitely superior to that in which these people lived previously. Yet the minister does not say: We are going to do better in the future and learn from the mistakes we made. He says: We will suspend these projects. We are not going to go ahead with them in the near future. Nothing more disastrous for the ordinary people of this country has been said by a minister of the Crown since world war II. The task force goes on to say at page 57 of its report:
As a further alternative to public housing, serious consideration should be given to a program of income supplements to permit low income families to rent or even purchase housing according to their own needs in the private market.
As long as we have the tremendous shortage of housing that we have at the present time, what will a supplement for low income people mean in the field of housing? I suggest that what it will mean is very obvious. It will mean a bonanza, a gift to landlords, particularly slum landlords. If this is what the minister is proposing, without a very substantial increase in total housing starts, particularly total housing starts for low income people, it will not mean very much to the ordinary Canadian citizen. The minister and the task force are proposing, in effect, a gift to people who are already making a substantial profit on their investment. Let me quote from a Financial Times news service item which was reprinted in the Winnipeg Tribune of May 1, 1968:
Despite the widespread increases in wages last year, landlords and bond investors, not wage earners, made the biggest gains in income.
Kent, interest and miscellaneous investment income rose nearly 13 per cent in 1967, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics reports. Wages and salaries averaged only a 9 per cent increase.
The minister is not addressing himself to the problem of providing more public housing, more housing for rent at prices which the

March 4, 1969
Business of Supply
ordinary person in the low income group can afford. Instead the minister proposes to stop this program temporarily-and we know how long "temporary" can be with this government. The report of the task force, which was of such high priority that the minister was absent from the house literally for weeks on end, has now been before us for almost six weeks and there is no indication at all that the government intends to bring forward legislation in the near future implementing the supposedly good recommendations contained in the report. The minister proposes that rent supplements be paid to tenants. I suggest this will immediately lead to increases in rents because landlords know that there is a shortage of housing accommodation.
The minister said a number of things last night which it is almost impossible to believe were said in a serious way. He said the government had commissioned a study by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to ascertain what the effect of a shortage of housing accommodation would be on the cost of purchase or rent of living accommodation. One does not have to be very wise to understand what will happen. The Liberal government believes in a laissez-faire economy and the law of supply and demand. Therefore it knows that if there is a shortage, as there is, of housing accommodation, the price of housing will stay at its increased level. The government knows that if houses are built for sale or rent in large quantities and there is a surplus, which we have not had for 30 years and probably will not have for another 20, the price of housing will go down.
The minister thought that what the government had done was great. He talked about the advantages of imposing on land developers a capital gains tax on unearned increment. My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre heard this and said that although the minister may not have accepted socialism yet he may come to that point 50 years from now because he has accepted Henry George's single tax idea. What good is it if the Minister of Transport, who is in charge of housing, thinks it is a good idea? We would like to know what the Minister of Finance thinks of this idea. We would like to know when we will have the kind of capital gains tax which was proposed several years ago by the Carter commission.
The minister and the task force have been great in making recommendations about

things over which the minister and the government have no control. The task force made a whole host of recommendations about matters which are clearly the responsibility of the provincial governments. About these, of course, the minister waxed eloquent, as did the task force. We have to take into account what I consider to be the harsh, completely uncalled for, negative approach of the minister and the task force to the problems of public housing. The hon. member for Davenport mentioned that there are in Toronto a very large number of people who need housing. The same is true of Montreal, Winnipeg and Hamilton.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am indebted to the house for this opportunity to discuss Bill C-173 for a few minutes. I shall not deal with the clause concerning housing but with that one regarding the estimates for the Department of Forestry and Rural Development which will soon become the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I also thank the minister for being in the house at the present time and I would like to give him the assurance that my remarks will be as brief as possible.
If I asked to have the floor, Mr. Chairman, it is because I must be in my constituency tomorrow in order to attend a debate on the unemployment insurance arbitration board, and when Bill C-173 is examined again next week, I shall have to go away once more for the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, of which I am a member, will be meeting in several NATO countries.
March 4, 1969

So, Mr. Chairman, the question I want to raise this evening concerns a vast portion of the Northern Territories, not the Northwest Territories as such, but the territories north of Quebec, comprising Abitibi and what is usually called Northwestern Quebec.
Recently, I attended in Rouyn a symposium organized by social workers to make the government aware of the needs of the people of that area and try to find a solution to the problems faced by too many people of that vast area. There, I found out from data supplied at the meeting that over 40,000 people live on hand-outs from the Department of National Health and Welfare. As the total population is about 165,000, it means that 25 per cent of the population must depend on the Department of National Health and Welfare payments to live. Moreover, this does not include the many people living off unemployment insurance benefits, and many more whose income is inadequate to meet their obligations and also maintain a decent standard of living. So that is the situation prevailing in Northwestern Quebec now.
Some businessmen have suggested to start new industries to provide employment for the people of that area and to stabilize the industrial economy of Abitibi. But these men must face all the problems of competition against other areas getting better aid from the federal government. In fact, I see on the list of designated areas that Abitibi is surrounded by a sort of horse shoe. All around areas may benefit from the lesiglation on designated areas act, while my own area of Abitibi is not eligible.
Why? Because the unemployment rate, according to the criteria used up to now, and the employment rate in our area would seem adequate to prevent it from being declared a designated area.
I wished to open the debate tonight because I believed that the new department to be entrusted to the present Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand) will have more leeway to decide which areas should get grants to improve labour conditions.
Since we shall no more speak of designated areas but rather of special areas, I wish to call the minister's attention to the urgency of considering northwestern Quebec as an area whose population is in great need of assistance to attract industries that will provide work for the unemployed. Those people have to content themselves with public assistance, and theirs is the fate that awaits the young people soon to leave school.
Business of Supply
Our region is now endowed with fine secondary schools which qualify our young people for the CEGEP or -the university. They will want to go on with their studies and get degrees so that they may be able afterwards to put their knowledge at the service of their fellow-citizens. But if we fail to develop our resources these young people will go somewhere else, to other areas, to other provinces and maybe to other countries to find employment.
So, Mr. Chairman, it is urgent that the Canadian government should do everything possible to recognize this region as a designated area which will permit it to avail itself of its share of taxes so that its people may progress and find there the employment and economic welfare to which they are entitled.
A few months ago, a conference was held in Val-d'Or and the main speaker was Mr. Richard Rohmer, a Toronto lawyer and board chairman of the Foundation of the Middle North of Canada. I feel that this rather recent foundation is called upon to obtain great achievements in the near future. This is Mr. Rohmer's statement on that occasion and I quote:
The inheritance of Canada is made up of its lands of the North and the Middle North. It is in those areas that is found our great wealth in national resources at ground level or underground. It is from the North and the Middle North that flows most of our economic power, the blood which will enable Canada to develop and prosper.
Mr. Chairman, I found that those words apply perfectly well to the northwestern area of Quebec which abounds in natural wealth of all kinds, forest, mines as well as people. The development of those natural resources would enable the entire country to profit therefrom.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I will continue to read from the statements made by Mr. Rohmer on that occasion, because I feel that they are quite important. I quote:
There will be about 100 million people in Canada in the year 2067. The figures come from a study of the present increase in population, that is by immigration and births, and are based on data from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
Considering the data, there must be a collective effort all over the country to establish and organize a long-term economic development plan for the utilization of the lands and resources of the inhabitable regions of the Middle North. Otherwise, our population will be concentrated along the border with the United States, particularly in the Great Lakes region.
Mr. Chairman, government support is often requested for the development of some areas and, from time to time, we hear ministers or

March 4, 1969
Business of Supply
heads of government say that the population must not rely on government assistance only,
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, this remark by no means applies to the people of Abitibi, since it is the third winter that works are undertaken and financed exclusively by these people in order to build, as far as James Bay, a road which will be the first to join the south to the sea. It is the people of Abitibi themselves with their own resources, who cleared the land in order to build a road to the sea. No help has been granted so far by the government. This proves, Mr. Chairman, that the people in north-west Quebec are not lazy and do not rely on the help of the government, even if it is said and rightly so perhaps, that at the moment, the principal industry in Abitibi is social welfare. The people demonstrated with the help of businessmen and the general support, that they wish to develop their resources and their territory in order to place it at the disposal of all people.
At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say why we want to develop our region. We do not ask the government to finance these developments alone, but rather to help those people who have already started to clear new territories so that our young people may settle there before others do so. I would now like to quote an article that was published in the paper La Frontiere, on the 6th of December 1967:
It is useless to open lands if trade and industry are not promoted to the same extent in order to absorb the products and the surplus of manpower.
One must go where natural resources are to be found. It is impossible to maintain artificially the economy of a region by vague promises and low subsidies.
The benefits to the people of the Northwest of this road-
-which is already under construction-
*-can be summarized under three main headings:
A-Mines
B-Forests
C-Trade and tourism
A. Where mining is concerned, this road will open to the people of the Northwest and of the province of Quebec in general, a new area of prospection and development, available to all, whether by land or by sea. Cape Smith is surrounded with mountains of asbestos and nickel. The Trinity or Belcher islands have countless fields of magnetic iron and copper. Close to the Big Whale River, there are beds of lead and zinc. There are fantastic oil fields under the Phelypeaux islands. There is plenty of natural gas along James Bay. The limestone of the Phelypeaux islands is just as wonderful as the limestone you find in the Paris area.

Prospectors hired by the Selco Exploration Ltd. and by two other Canadian companies, the Canadian Rock Co. and Hard Metal (Canada) Ltd., are now digging for diamonds in the vicinity of James Bay and Hudson Bay. I guess this is enough-
Mr. Chairman, this is likely to arouse the interest of businessmen and governments in this area so 'as to make it available to the people who want to develop it. He goes on:
As for lumbering this road will open to our lumber contractors the invaluable wealth of forests located along the rivers flowing into James Bay. Trees there are now fullgrown and it is high time they should be felled.
I gather from a recent study conducted by Michel Cice, an engineering expert, that it would be possible to set up three more pulp and paper mills in this vast area, and about 100 saw mills to process lumber.
You may well imagine Mr. Chairman, the inexhaustible opportunities for lumbering in this territory.
I go on quoting:
C-If we now consider trade and tourism, this road, while giving access to the Arctic and Atlantic oceans will enable our people to expand into an area hitherto out of reach because of prohibitive costs.
Huge commercial fisheries can then develop into a profitable enterprise the best fish in the world, that of the Arctic ocean. By considerably speeding up deliveries and exchanges in the James and Hudson Bays, this road will gradually promote trade.
The North Sea has now been spoken of for over 300 years. Needless to say once the road is completed, it will become an irresistible tourist attraction.
Mr. Chairman, I have pointed out these facts to the new Minister of Regional Economic Expansion this evening to give him all the reasons needed to recognize the northwestern area of Quebec as a special area so that it might obtain the required subsidies for the businessmen, the industrialists who wish to set up new industries, or process on the spot the resources found there, such as forests and mines.
As I pointed out to the minister last year, we cannot be expected, because of the distance that separates us from the large centres, to import raw materials to process them and then export them. We must therefore endeavour to develop and process our natural resources where we find them and then offer them to the Canadian or foreign consumers.
Mr. Chairman, I feel therefore that the Canadian government, through its minister, should study carefully the proposals submitted tonight and fully support the development of northwestern Quebec and, in particular, the construction of the access road from
March 4, 196J	COMMONS
Abitibi towards James Bay so that the natural resources located there can be developed.
Being a member of the committee on Indian affairs and northern development, I know that the government spends rather large amounts of money for the development of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I agree with the efforts the government makes to help them develop. I know that 40 per cent of the exploration costs in those two areas are paid for by the federal government.
I therefore feel that the government could put relatively large amounts of money at the disposal of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion for the development of the Abitibi region, that this area might also participate in the economic development we are witnessing in Canada today, so that its inhabitants, who want to live there and develop the area, can enjoy the same standard of living as other Canadians as well as the same advantages.
Mr. Chairman, I make those remarks for the information of the minister trusting that he will turn a ready ear to them and give effect to them.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on July 17, 1968, the cabinet of the newly formed Government of Canada met and decided to establish a task force to look into the problem of housing in Canada. The transport minister was appointed to act as leader of that task force, the terms of reference of which were to examine housing and urban development in Canada and report on any way in which the federal government, in company with other levels of government and the private sector, could help meet the housing needs of all Canadians and contribute to the development of modern, vital cities. In theory, all this sounded beautiful. With a great burst of publicity the task force kicked off some time in August or September. For a short time it was impossible to turn on a television set or pick up a newspaper without seeing either the smiling face of the Minister of Transport or his sideburns, depending on the angle of the camera. I confess that the face was not an unpleasant one.
When the task force was set up the Canadian people were led to believe that finally, after many years, something would be done to solve our housing crisis. The task force took on the appearance of a travelling entertainment show or highly publicized circus, one might say. Unfortunately, the report it brought down did not live up to our expectations. The only tangible product of all the trips the task force made was an evening film show presented in a partially darkened room with a spotlight on the minister's face. We saw various slides of the housing situation across the country and heard a solemn voice describing the adverse conditions that were found.
Some recommendations of the report sounded reasonable enough, and I wish to talk about two or three of them. I wish to begin with the problem of interest rates. Speaking to the national conference of the Canadian Home Manufacturers Association, the minister said in Toronto on January 13, in part:
As an indication of the achievement of the housing program between 1951 and 1961, the number of dwellings without a piped water supply declined from 26 per cent to 5.5 per cent-and more importantly between 1949 and 1964 the average cost for an NHA bungalow increased 36.8 per cent while disposable income per capita went up 87.2 per cent. Because the rise in incomes exceeded

March 4, 1969
Business of Supply
that of housing prices, the working man in Canada had the opportunity of buying and owning his own home.
I point out that the period when housing was in adequate supply ended in 1964, one year after the Liberal government returned to power. The minister went on to say:
Then a series of converging forces altered that favourable position. Housing starts in 1966 fell off drastically. In 1964 and 1965 there was an average of 165,000 housing starts. In 1966, this fell to 134,474. The culprit was largely rising interest rates that drew money out of the mortgage field and generally forced up costs.
I am glad the minister recognizes that the major culprit in our housing problem is high interest rates. It is, therefore, a paradox to find the minister recommending as item No. 5 in the report of the task force that:
The interest rate for insured loans under the National Housing Act be freed to find its own level in the financial marketplace.
That recommendation is not in keeping with the speech he made on January 13. If interest rates are to find their own level they will go up.
Next, I wish to speak about the recommendation regarding the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. The Canadian people were pleased when the minister announced he thought the 11 per cent sales tax ought to be removed. It must be remembered that similar announcements had been made during the election campaign in June. It does not seem that that recommendation will be carried out, however. Only a day or two after the task force report was tabled or released the Minister of Finance was asked whether he would agree to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. He stood up and said simply, no. He offered no explanation for his refusal. Here we have a senior cabinet minister recommending something one day and the very next day another senior cabinet minister saying no to this recommendation. To me that does not represent cabinet solidarity. If there is disagreement in the cabinet, the country suffers.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The third aspect I would deal with is the problem of housing, particularly with reference to people living in conditions of poverty. I would place in this group Metis, Indians and many white people with low incomes. Under the present legislation, N.H.A. mortgages are not available to people who earn
[Mr. Yewchuk.l
less than $8,200 a year. I venture to say this covers more than half the working population of Canada. It includes Indians and the vast majority of Metis people as well as farmers who live on small mixed farms on the prairies. It also includes the vast majority of the labour force in the towns and cities.
The report does not offer a solution to the problem of housing faced by these people. With regard to the Indian people, the situation is not as difficult. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development realized there was a problem and set up a program which I would suggest the Minister of Transport examine. The department assists the Indian people to build houses, not expensive houses but more or less up to date houses with most of the modern conveniences which people expect. On a reservation an Indian must provide $500 worth of work or cash and the balance is financed by the department. In this way the Indian becomes the proud owner of a new home.
In Alberta there are several colonies of Metis people which are administered by the Metis rehabilitation branch. There is a housing problem for these people who live in the colonies which allows them to receive a new house under similar circumstances. These people must also pay a certain amount of money, approximately $500, either in the form of cash, labour or materials and the balance is financed by the provincial government.
The program for Indian people is carried on in areas other than on reserves. If an Indian person is working away from the reservation he is still entitled to the benefits of this housing program. Most people do not realize the difference between Indians and Metis. Most of the colonies are not economically sound areas. They are presumably set up as agriculture areas and are not self-supporting. The Metis are forced to live in colonies to qualify for new houses. If they work in urban areas some distance away they are forced to live in a colony in order to get a new house. I am familiar with some Metis people who must commute 30 to 50 miles to their place of employment. I suggest that Metis people should qualify for houses away from colonies in the same way they qualify in colonies. The regulations should be similar to those for the Indian people who qualify for housing although they do not live on reservations. This would solve the problem for many Metis people. There is no reason why such a program should be restricted to Metis people. It
March 4, 1969



should also be available to those who have only temporary employment or for one reason or another do not have high incomes. These programs are financed by federal and provincial government funds.
I was a little upset with one of the recommendations of the task force that, to some extent, public housing should be discontinued for the present. The suggestion is that until a study is made of the various psychological and sociological factors affecting people who live in public housing, no major starts in public housing should be made. I wonder if this is a good suggestion. I am inclined to think it is dangerous as it may remove the possibility of certain people in low income groups having adequate housing when there is no reasonable alternative plan. I hope public housing is not discontinued in the same way as the winter works program. The country was led to believe the winter works program would be replaced by a better program, but as yet nothing has been done.
I conclude my remarks by saying that the task force did produce a lot of useful information. Canadian people were led to believe that the problems of housing would certainly be solved, not necessarily quickly but positive suggestions would evolve. I am sorry to say that I have not seen any such results. This task force was another big hoax perpetrated on the public of Canada in the same way as the one on June 25. I hope the minister responsible for housing takes into consideration some of the suggestions put forward today and makes an honest and earnest effort to solve this major problem faced by Canadians.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1969
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have heard unkind words about the housing policy of this government and the minister responsible for housing during the past weeks, days, hours and minutes. Wild charges have been flung with abandon around the chamber. We have heard the words "hoax", "folly" and "fraud". These are very serious terms to be employed by responsible public servants. We have heard people such as the hon. member for Winnipeg North suggest that the housing task force report contains a recommendation that public housing in this country be abandoned. This afternoon we heard the suggestion that government is reneging on its responsibility to those in the unfortunate position of attempting to support a family on a marginal income.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
This is totally irresponsible talk. The serious aspect about it is that it is causing serious
Business of Supply
concerns in the minds and hearts of low income families across the country. These are unjustifiable concerns. When an elected member of parliament stands up in his place and makes a statement that fraud is being perpetrated then he should be able to justify his remarks, but so far in this debate we have not heard any evidence advanced.
Yesterday, referring to the housing task force report, the hon. member for Greenwood assured all of us that "the document is a colossal flop," and the hon. member for Broadview told us the report is "a fraud". To be charitable, and it is difficult to be charitable after listening to this line of debate, and one can only suggest that members in the opposition, at least a number because some of them are ordinarily responsible, have failed to read the report and study its contents. We know them. We have heard them attempt to stir up the fires of division in this country. In this debate, their contribution has hardly added to the sum total of human knowledge and understanding of the task force report, the most important document produced on housing since Confederation.
The cabinet made its decision on July 17 last. There had been a great deal of criticism prior to that date. Members in the opposition had said, "This is a do nothing government. They are doing nothing about the housing problem." Some of them said, "What we want is a study of the problem." Then, the study was commenced on July 17, authorizing the Minister of Transport to establish a task force on housing, "which would report to him within six months starting in September."
The minister then proceeded to carry out this authorization, and he did so with dispatch. He established the terms of reference for the task force. Then of course criticism began to come from the opposition. Opposition members asked, "Why is the government studying the problem when it should be acting the way we would if we were charged with responsibility?" The opposition line changed. The concensus was that we did not need a task force, that instead we needed action.

-"to examine housing and urban development in Canada and to report on ways in which the federal government, in company with other levels of government and the private sector, can help meet the housing needs of all Canadians and contribute to the development of modern, vital cities."

I think it is unfortunate-

This nation, which is supposed to be a haven for this government which is perpetrating fraud, built 200,000 housing units in 1968. is too bad that the schedules of apposition members did not permit them to attend, to watch the task force in action and see the Minister of Transport who undertook a difficult job. I came away with the same conclusion as did the task force, that low income families need more help, but surely society can do more than condemn them to a housing ghetto.
Some of the statements which we heard at the Skeena Terrace project-and it is a good project of its type-were statements that I would not want to repeat on the floor of this house because they were framed in such bitterness and such disillusionment that they would shock many people. Severe and damaging results have ensued to many families in housing projects. Then, we might turn to page 55 of the report. I am afraid perhaps the pages in the copies which some of the opposition members have are stuck together because their copies have never been opened. I find 'at page 43 of the housing task force report, which is condemned in such bitter terms in this debate, that there are measures advanced to provide generous financial assistance to meet the housing crisis. What is the number one point in the New Democratic party platform on housing? It is to provide generous financial assistance to meet the housing crisis. Then, the second recommendation is to bring down the cost of mortgage money. When I turn to the task force report I find four proposals to bring down the cost of mortgage money. That is point number two in the New Democratic party platform. Then, their platform reads:
Support the principle of integrated community development so that transportation, schools, recreation and shopping facilities are developed together with new and renewed housing.
Lo and behold, when we turn to page 55 of the housing task force report we find this:
There are obvious limits as to what can be done by way of physical restructuring. But the members would suggest that every effort be made to utilize vacant or redevelopment space within the immediate area to relieve some of the present shortcomings for recreational facilities and open space.

-where I find the following:
The Federal Government, in co-operation with a provincial government, should seriously consider the construction of a "new city'' as a pilot project-
Yet, as we know, this is a report condemned out of hand by the socialist members of this house. Despite that, it contains all the four main points in the N.D.P. platform for the last election campaign. We might ask what are the real motives of some of the critics and do they have a greater interest in amassing votes for a national election than in a real concern about serving the housing needs of the Canadian people? They have referred to the housing task force report as a hoax and a fraud. Does that mean that the New Democratic party platform is a hoax and a fraud?
We, on the government side, do not believe that the status quo needs to be defended. We say there is nothing sacred about the existing housing program. The only thing wrong with it is it could be made better. The task force has said, the minister has said, and government members 'agree that the present public housing program is not good enough. This does not mean a total withdrawal of the government from public housing projects, a partial withdrawal or any withdrawal. In fact, it means an expansion of the existent program with changes in style, design and layout- changes which would make shelter for low income families more compatible with family living.
Does a de-emphasis on public housing as we know it now mean a callous retrenchment as has been suggested? It means, among other things, that there will be more emphasis on limited dividend and co-operative housing and more help for these plans. Does the task force's concern about the social implications of the present style of public housing mean that this government is turning its back on the problems of the elderly, the students or Canadians of Indian and Metis origin? On the contrary, the special programs will go ahead with increased emphasis, support and determination by this government.
The sum total of the task force recommendations will make it easier for the working

March 4. 1969
Business of Supply
man and his family to buy decent shelter. This will be the result despite the contrived efforts of some members of the opposition to brand the report as a fraud before its recommendations have been weighed, tested or, I suspect, even read by most of them. This report says there are alternatives to the bleak multi-family high rise accommodation in Canada. It points out that Canadian technology, design, planning, engineering and finance can find better solutions to the shelter needs of the low income groups in our midst. It states that we need not be bound by concepts of the past.
We have been told the task force report constitutes fraud and folly. Was it fraud for the task force to say, as it did:
Urgency. That certainly is among the strongest of the Task Force impressions. The need to act while reasonable action is still possible. Many Canadians, whose needs are of yesterdays, want adequate housing today and not tomorrow. Theirs is the voice of frustration that no longer will accept the explanation that it is "that other" government's responsibility to act. Theirs is the growing anger of people who, amid the material plenty around them, refuse to wait that "little bit longer" for their minimal share.
This is what has been branded as fraud and folly. I agree with what the task force said. Any reasonable member in this house will agree with it. Was it fraud for this allegedly cold-hearted task force to say:
The Task Force is convinced that Canada has the resources, material, technological and intellectual, to meet these needs and problems. To believe otherwise is to despair and surrender to the inevitable.
Yet, there are members in this house who want to enshrine the status quo and who believe that public housing must be beyond criticism. Thank goodness we have some responsible groups in this country, like the urban renewal administrators of Canada, who endorsed the report in Winnipeg over the week end. That is one source that has never been quoted by the opposition.
Is it fraud and folly to suggest that the government encourage private lending institutions and growing pension funds to become more involved in making money available for housing? Is it fraud and folly to suggest that the federal government consider the establishment of savings and mortgage institutions to serve the residential mortgage market on a regional basis? Is it fraud and folly to propose a central mortgage bank to provide additional liquidity for existing lending institutions? Is it fraud and folly to free the
[Mr. Perrault.l
interest rate? Is it irresponsible to propose alternate forms of insured loans under the National Housing Act to provide greater flexibility for lenders and borrowers?
Is it wrong to suggest that the maximum loan ceiling under the National Housing Act should be substantially increased? Is this fraud, when at the outset some 20,000 new Canadian families would qualify for loans because of this measure? In addition, there is the lengthening of the amortization period of the loans. Let these housing critics tell us of the fraud involved in the task force recommendation that down payments should be progressively reduced so that middle and lower income groups can obtain modest housing under a lease-purchase system without initial equity participation. We have been told that this is a hoax and an attempt to mislead the low income families. What about the proposal that purchasers of existing homes should be entitled to comparable mortgage conditions under the National Housing Act to those which apply to new homes. Is this a fraud? Is it fraudulent to suggest that insurance fees, legal charges, real estate commissions and other administrative costs be reduced and that the school tax should be removed from the family home?
Where is the fraud and the folly when the task force concerns itself with the low income groups once again by suggesting that greater encouragement be given to the use of limited dividend, non-profit and co-operative projects as a means of providing adequate accommodation for lower income groups? Does this report deserve to be condemned out of hand when it proposes that the federal government should make direct loans to municipalities or regional governments to assist them in assembling and servicing land for urban growth?
I should like to conclude, Mr. Chairman, by saying that the task force report is a document well worth study and consideration. Those who assembled it are good, conscientious Canadians who deserve something better than to be accused of fraud by certain members in this house. Opposition has a duty to oppose that which is wrong or contrary to the public interest. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, it has another duty, a duty to be fair and a duty to be responsible. Some of the criticism heard during the past weeks, months and days is not fair. It is an attempt not to be fair. Surely, we are sent to this place to make a more constructive contribution to public life.
March 4, 1969

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in following the remarks of the hon. member for Bumaby-Seymour, and at the risk of being accused of stirring up differences of opinion and dissension across the country, I should like to put a few things of interest on record during this debate on the task force on housing and certain recommendations contained in their report.
The hon. member, in his usual way, asked members of the house to refer to page 55 of the report. He suggested that perhaps these pages in the reports of hon. members in the opposition had stuck together since we had not read them. I would ask that hon. member to refer to page 48. I suggest that the Minister of Transport responsible for housing and the members of the cabinet probably had the pages of their copies at this point stuck or glued together. At page 48, the task force recommended that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials be abolished. I suggest that this recommendation has been a source of embarrassment to the minister and the government.
The Minister of Finance has already stated that despite the recommendation of the task force and the Minister of Transport responsible for housing, the government will not remove this sales tax. I am sure we all appreciate the fact that the Minister of Transport had the foresight and the courage to suggest to his colleagues in cabinet that the 11 per cent sales tax be removed. We regret that his colleagues have not had the same charitable feeling toward the people of Canada, and have not agreed with the minister in respect of the removal of this sales tax. In my
Business of Supply
opinion, the minister has been repudiated by his colleagues and his recommendations have been pushed aside.
This is a very worthwhile recommendation, and I am sure when this report was tabled some time ago all Canadians, especially those in the middle and low income groups, were delighted to know that this 11 per cent sales tax would probably be abolished. The joy was short lived. I am sorry to note that this has not been done. Members on this side of the house are very disappointed that the government has refused to accept this recommendation. Obviously, this government intends to maintain this sales tax.
This sales tax is a very important factor to married couples or people in the low or middle income range, particularly when it comes to building or buying homes. The 11 per cent sales tax adds about $500 or $600 to the cost of a home. This can make the difference between a person being able to afford to build a house and a person being unable to do so. I suggest that the government should reconsider the removal of this 11 per cent sales tax.
Another recommendation made in this report deals with the mortgage insurance fund. Most members know that this fund was set up in respect of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Originally, it was established so that people who obtained mortgages through the National Housing Act would be assessed 2 per cent of the amount of the mortgage, which amount was in turn set aside in a special fund. The task force report suggests that this amount be reduced by half. The recommendation is that it should be 1 per cent instead of 2 per cent.
Since the establishment of this fund in 1954, $224 million have been accumulated. One wonders why this fund is necessary. Since the inception of the National Housing Act 800,000 loans have been made. I understand there have been 6,700 claims against this insurance fund. Most of these claims have resulted from the situation which developed in the Elliott Lake area. I understand also that most of the houses which were repossessed there, or had foreclosure action taken against them, have since been sold or are in the process of being sold.
I would certainly recommend to the minister and the government that we should try to make housing available to the middle and low income groups. If we want to help people in those income brackets, there is one tangible way in which it can be done. We can do away

March 4, 1969
Business of Supply
with the 2 per cent charge that is now being assessed for the mortgage insurance fund.
I have mixed feelings in respect of public housing because we all know certain sociological problems are involved. We all know what has happened in some large cities. I know particularly what has happened in the city of St. John's. We have some excellent public housing complexes, but there are others which have become nothing more than ghettoes. This is one of the dangers in respect of public housing under the present concept.
One of the problems facing these people who occupy these subsidized rental units is related to the fact that rent is assessed on the basis of their gross income. This is very unfair in my opinion. I can cite hundreds of cases which occurred in 1968, particularly during the wintertime, when many individuals earned a certain amount of money as a result of working overtime. I understand their rent will be based on the amount of money they earned in 1968. This is very unfair because in 1968 these people earned this amount of money because they worked a considerable amount of overtime. This additional income is being added to the income they earn in 1969 for the purposes of assessing their 1969 rents. As a result, a hardship is being imposed on these people.
These people are being charged rent based on 27 per cent of their regular incomes in 1968. But because of the additional earnings throughout overtime worked in that year, the assessed rents in the following year could well amount to 30 per cent or more of their gross income. I contend this destroys the initiative of these people and discourages them from getting out to work a few hours overtime or to develop some part time employment. They are discouraged when they realize that of every dollar they earn as a result of overtime or a part time job 27 per cent is deducted and applied to their rent.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I would ask the Minister of Transport and his colleagues to give serious thought to changing the method by which rents are assessed in respect of people who live in subsidized rental accommodation. I think the present method is unfair and does not give the people concerned any opportunity to save a down payment and eventually buy a house.
The report makes several recommendations with regard to urban renewal schemes, studies, and so on. Having served for a number

of years on the city council of St. John's, I am well aware of the red tape involved in trying to get an urban renewal or land development scheme off the ground. I know that a certain procedure must be followed. It is only reasonable to assume that this should be so. But I know from experience that a great deal of unnecessary hardship has been caused by typical civil service bureaucracy, typical civil service red tape. This should be eliminated if cities are to avail themselves of the urban renewal benefits of the National Housing Act.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour is very upset over some remarks made on this side of the house. He was almost crying for a few minutes. I found it almost impossible to avoid filling up, but thank goodness I recovered and could stand up and say a few words. I am the first to agree that in this report there are several worth-while recommendations. However, I do not think it is enough for a task force on housing, that has travelled the length and breadth of Canada at great public expense, to make many recommendations and not as yet have one implemented.

speechtext: Except cutting down public housing.

speechtext:
Interest rates have increased. The suggestion that the sales tax be removed has been thrown out. I suggest to the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour that it is not enough for the government to commission a task force on housing to travel the country and study the problems which the average and low income people are facing with regard to housing, and then to do nothing about those problems. This report, which has been compiled at great expense to the Canadian taxpayer, is only as good as the attitude which the government in power adopts towards the recommendations made. If the government treats the other recommendations as it has the one that the sales tax be eliminated, I suggest we might as well throw the report out, because then it will be useless.
Flowery phrases and recommendations will not alleviate the problems facing the people in my riding, many of whom are living in homes that are not fit for human habitation. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that unless the government takes this report seriously and finds some way to implement the recommendations contained therein, the minister's trip across the country will have been unecessary and a waste of public money. I suggest to the Minister and his colleagues that the co-operative housing concept should be studied. This
March 4, 1969

is a program that enables a person who is not afraid to take off his coat and roll up his shirt sleeves, to go to work for himself and build his own home with government assistance. I can cite cases in my province and city where from 1951 to 1955 hundreds of new homes were built through the co-operative housing movement. This is a scheme whereby 9, 10 or 12 people get together, study building methods and ideas, financing methods, and so on, and then apply to Central Mortgage and Housing, through the province, and receive a commitment for a mortgage. They then go to it and build their own homes in the co-operative fashion, by buying co-operatively, in bulk, and thereby effecting considerable savings. This is one idea I would like the government to study. It should see if the co-operative housing concept in home building cannot be encouraged and taken advantage of by more middle income, middle class Canadians.
Those of us who live in the less fortunate provinces of Canada are well aware of the suffering and misery faced by people living in substandard homes. We agree that much has been done in this respect. Public housing projects have been built. But in many respects I think we have only scratched the surface, and a great deal more remains to be done. I believe it is obvious that the government must take the leadership and adopt policies that will help the average Canadian obtain a decent home for himself and his family.
I was very interested in the words of Dr. Albert Rose, professor at the University of Toronto, who said that the most important change that could be made in our national housing policy would be a formal declaration that the federal and provincial governments intended, during the balance of this century, to discriminate in favour of families and individuals at the bottom half of the income distribution. This is a very thought-provoking observation, because it is obvious that it is the sort of thing this government must do. The government must, in the balance of this century, discriminate in favour of the people who have been suffering for too long because they have lived in substandard housing. I hope that the Prime Minister's promise of a just society will embrace the proposition of providing reasonable and cheaper homes for people who are deserving of them.
These are the things I would like to see done in the next few weeks, Mr Chairman. I would like to see the government take the Minister of Transport off the hook, give him back his pride and allow him to again stand
Business of Supply
tall and walk straight. When he makes a recommendation to the cabinet, I hope they will accept his recommendation. With respect to this report, which was compiled at great personal sacrifice to the minister and at great expense to the Canadian taxpayer, I hope it will not be shelved, thrown aside, and its recommendations ignored. Let the government tell the people of Canada that it takes the Minister of Transport seriously, will reconsider its decision, and in fact abolish the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. Let the government show the people of Canada that it means business. It can do this by abolishing the 2 per cent insurance fee in respect of mortgages.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
These are some of the things which could be done, and I hope for the sake of the less fortunate Canadians that steps are taken to make money available to people in lower-middle income groups to help them get housing. Under the National Housing Act at the present time, Mr. Chairman, a person who wishes to get an $18,000 mortgage must be earning in excess of $8,000 a year. When one considers that in many cities in Canada-I could name one-less than 5 per cent, perhaps, and certainly less than 10 per cent are in this category, we begin to realize what this means. What hope is there for the other 90 per cent? More than 90 per cent of our people cannot qualify for a National Housing mortgage. The recommendations contained in the report that the maximum should be increased and the amortization period extended are excellent suggestions and I hope the minister and the government will implement them.

speechtext:
Before I begin the main part of my speech this evening, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour on his fine defence of New Democratic party housing policy. I hope it will be my privilege to do as good a job, though I promise I shall not be half as loud.
We heard a fine speech in defence of the various proposals in the report of the task force but we are living in a fool's paradise because as yet we have not seen any legislation arising from the report. When such legislation has been brought forward we may be more confident that what is contained in the report will become a reality for most Canadians.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour told us the report had been defended by at least one authority. I have quotations here from several authorities who have been

are below these levels, little or nothing is provided. Mr. Chairman, we shall be forced into a change of attitude in this regard. People who are earning less than $8,000 a year will not tolerate for ever living in grim, jerry-built suites in cities or driving back and forth a hundred miles a day to work. I have people in my constituency who drive this distance to work and who are forced to live in unsatisfactory accommodation in trailer camps without adequate facilities, simply because we have not done enough soon enough.
The housing problem is really an income problem. There is no evidence that people with unlimited incomes have any problem at all with regard to housing. They do not suffer from the housing shortage and by and large neither do those who already own a house. But young families today, growing families, desperately need more accommodation. As the task force report says, all Canadians should be entitled to clean, warm shelter as a matter of basic human right. I hope that this is not just another empty gesture but is a principle that the government will follow when it brings down its legislation. If it does not do so, I am certain there will be many disillusioned people in Canada in addition to the ones we have at the moment.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
In the province from which I come, British Columbia, the people who need public housing or financial assistance the most are not receiving it in their fair proportion under the N.H.A. legislation. If I might just put some statistics on the record, of the lower one third of the population income group in 1967 only 5.7 per cent received any C.M.H.C. funds at all. Here again is the application of socialism for the affluent.
The problem is also very serious in the community in which I live, Coquitlam. The local social welfare administration reports to me that 85 per cent of people on social welfare receive rent subsidies in addition to welfare payments because accommodation is not available to them without such assistance. If they are spending extra money on rent, obviously they are unable to spend it on things they need like dental care, clothing, food, insurance and other items.
At the moment, housing is taking up far too large a proportion of most people's income. In the same community, in 1967, 1,200 new homes were constructed. Thus 1,200 new families moved into the community. In the same area the average purchase price of
Business of Supply
these 1,200 new homes was $25,000. Since the average income in British Columbia is $5,600 per year per family, I should like to ask what kind of families moved into these new homes. Again, this supports what I said earlier: National Housing Act money is available to people whose incomes are high enough to qualify for loans, but not available to those people who are desperately in need of housing.
I am an ex-municipal alderman and can see the desirability of attracting quality construction to the community. The assessments are higher for tax purposes and treasuries that are short of money benefit. In addition, such developments are visually attractive to the community. There are fewer schools required because there is not the high density that exists in other areas. There is also probably much less drain on the various social services; usually these income groups have fewer problems. There are fewer broken homes, and so on.
Some very fine people have moved into Coquitlam and they were attracted to this area for the same reason I was. I had to make a decision. I had to decide whether I wanted to spend my money close to my job and pay high taxes on real estate, or whether I should move out to Coquitlam and spend my money on gasoline and tires and drive to work in Vancouver. I decided on the latter course.
However, you cannot build a wall around a municipality and keep people out. It does not matter whether you build a zoning wall, a financial wall, or whether there is a gentleman's agreement to keep certain people out of certain subdivisions. Every urban area must make certain that it provides for a reasonable blend of single family dwellings and other types of accommodation. This is where we fall down. There are examples of all kinds of fine suburban dwellings, but there is only one price bracket. There is no new housing that is attractive and within the range of smaller families with lower incomes.
I do not think we can depend forever upon the concept of the filtering process. This is the process whereby those people who buy a new home move out of another home which becomes available for people in the lower income groups. I do not think that these houses will be available in sufficient quantities, and in addition this is not the way we should attack the problem. Although this process does take place, it is illogical to put it forward as a long-term proposition.
As I have said, one cannot blame the municipalities for wanting to attract high

Naturally, most Canadians with families prefer to live in single family dwellings. But, under present economic conditions they cannot do so.i If the government plans to house the unfortunate part of our population, let it bring in legislation permitting it to do so. Members of our party probably will support that legislation. If the government has no such plans I see no alternative to public housing for the increasing number of Canadians who will need it.
I should like to see a housing authority and department of urban affairs set up. Nobody likes the stigma attached to public housing projects. Surely, it will be wise for the government to decentralize its housing program, to plan, to buy older homes and to rent apartments in private apartments blocks. If it does these things, it will have the support of our party. But, if the minister does nothing he will be made very uncomfortable by our snapping, carnivorous fangs puncturing him in the region of his posterior.

Mr. Chairman, I had not
intended speaking in this debate, since I represent a riding in rural Ontario which is fortunate in having no housing shortage. Having listened to some speeches, I thought it appropriate that I should make known my thoughts and give the committee some of my views on the subject. While it is true that the Minister of Transport headed the housing task force, we ought to remember that its report is not his report alone. Of course, it is a government report; nevertheless, some reputable citizens helped in its drafting. They are fine businessmen, successful in their professions, and not all of them are of the Liberal persuasion. These businessmen, along with the minister, went across Canada, studied the problem and drew up a report which, although it may not meet with the approval of all, nevertheless is a report of experts in this field. Therefore, when opposition members apply the terms, "hoax," and "fraud" to the minister and the report they are also applying those unparliamentary terms to some reputable Canadian citizens. It is a pity to have members of the most exclusive club in Canada indulging in the unparliamentary practice of calling the Minister of Transport names.
Hon. members who may have read the biographies of members of the task force will see just how good a job the members of that force have been doing in Canada. I repeat, it was unparliamentary of hon. members to
Business of Supply
apply the terms "hoax" and "fraud" to the minister and to these people.
As a supporter of the government I will be the first to admit that everything is not 100 per cent with housing in Canada, and that many improvements could be introduced. The report suggested many improvements that could be effected. In my opinion, that report shows evidence of considerable thought and work and should be examined carefully so that our housing situation in future will be better than it is at the present or has been in the past.
If we accept the fact that not everything is 100 per cent with our housing, how does that give the opposition the right to say that housing in Canada is in terrible shape? Let me ask, where in the world is it in better shape?

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1969
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1969
speechtext: Is it not true that Canadians have the best housing in the world? Is it not also true that if the government is to be blamed for any of our shortcomings in housing it should be given credit for its positive achievements in the field of housing? On average, Canadians are better housed than are our neighbours to the south. I know many hon. members have been to the United States. Let them examine the slums of New York City and they will see how bad slums really can be.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1969
speechtext: Does that excuse our slums?

I will talk about our slums in a minute. If hon. members go south of our border they will see millions of people who breathe no fresh air, whose only glimpse of a piece of ground is the ground in a park. Or, if they do not visit New York let them visit Los Angeles, a considerable portion of which the negro population burned down two or three years ago, largely because much of their housing was in deplorable state.
We, on this side of the house, admit that many of our housing difficulties need to be remedied; yet our citizens have not begun burning down our cities. Let hon. members of the opposition go to Cincinnati or New York if they want to see deplorable housing conditions. Some members are to go to Europe. If they find time to drag themselves away from the night clubs of Piccadilly let them walk down to where the people live and they will see that the houses in London are not in the best of shape. Or, perhaps they will prefer Paris, a city I have visited many times. They

will see housing conditions there are deplorable. II they do not like Paris they can visit the great city of Vienna, and find the same thing. The fact remains that this terrible, this monstrous government that the opposition has been crucifying for the last couple of days has provided its citizens not only with the best housing in North America but in the world.

There are several items in the report with which I agree. I do not understand how anyone in the opposition can disagree with the suggestion that there should be land banks. It is impossible for me to comprehend any criticism of the government in this regard. The minister would be the first to acknowledge that land banks should have been set up long ago. We cannot turn back the clock, so we must borrow tomorrow in order to have cheaper land a year from now. People are constantly moving from rural to urban areas and much more housing will be needed in our cities.
Four or five years ago I had the privilege of recommending to the legislature in Toronto that mortgages on old buildings should be included in the National Housing Act. I certainly agree with the suggestion made by the minister and the task force in this connection. A building which is only three or four years of age is classified as old. I listened to part of the budget presented by the treasurer of the Province of Ontario who I know very well. All things being equal, it was a reasonably good budget. I suggest to the Minister of Transport that when he is talking to his colleague, the Minister of Finance, he should suggest that the possibility of interest on loans for housing being a deduction from income tax should be investigated. When our friends to the south allow interest payments on mortgages to be deductible for income tax purposes there is no reason why we should not allow that in Canada. Every government in Canada is floating around not knowing where to go in the financial field. We need new plans, and 1 am happy to be the first in this chamber tonight to give credit to the Ontario Provincial Treasurer who, in his budget speech today, suggested what will happen two years hence. I am now going to say something that perhaps will not be popular in this chamber. But I am going to suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, that as Canadians we must realize that while everybody deserves clean, warm shelter, as the report suggests, that does not mean that everybody should have the opportunity or indeed the right to own a house. There are some people, not only in Canada but throughout the world, who will never be able to afford houses.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, it is far cheaper for you and I to rent than to buy a
Business of Supply
house. Let us take the case of an average house in the city of Toronto costing $30,000. Let us take the cost of money today, whether you are borrowing it or lending it. For illustrative purposes let us say you are lending it, and it is worth 8 per cent. Eight per cent on $30,000 is $2,400 any way you add it up, and when you put taxes on top of that, repairs, depreciation of the house and all the other costs that go with ownership, you can see that it is cheaper to rent a house than to buy it. Some people just are not in the fortunate position of being able to put up the necessary amount of capital. We should realize that a certain percentage of the people will never be able to afford a house.
I have heard the moaning and groaning of the Opposition that people do not have enough money for the down payment on a house. If they have not enough money for a down payment, then they should not buy a house.
