Mr. Chairman, we have been treated to some schoolmarming tonight. It appears some hon. members are a great deal better at criticizing what other people say than they are at presenting positive thoughts of their own. I hope I do not fall into that trap. I think the task force on housing was long overdue. I am not going to criticize their efforts, nor the report itself, except to say it was too late, perhaps 20 years too late, and the task force members were forced into an almost panic situation.
I agree with the idea that there should be a land bank. This is something that should have been undertaken a long time ago. It may be too late to do it effectively now because the price of land around cities has sky-rocketed almost out of reach.
We do not live in Utopia, and I do not suppose we ever will, but that does not say that Canada cannot and should not be much better than it is. It gives me no pleasure whatever to look to tired, battle scarred Europe and say we are better with regard to housing than it, or to say we are better off in housing than South America. The truth is that we do not have housing that is either adequate or a credit to a vibrant young nation such as ours, with all our resources, energy, leadership, ambition and everything else at our disposal.
Housing in Canada, whether it is publicly owned or privately owned, is a disgrace. In so far as our native peoples are concerned, nine out of ten of them live in hovels. In the district that I represented before the last election there were 28 Indian reservations. If you think things could not be better in Canada all I suggest is that you go and visit any of

those reservations. If you can find any more than 10 per cent of those senior citizens of Canada living in decent habitation, I will apologize to this committee. This is not because I did not try to correct the situation, and I did not leave because I was chased out. I am still welcome on all of those 28 Indian reservations because I sincerely feel for those people, and I strongly urge that we do something to help them.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I suggest that the task force, whether or not they did it in the form of a specific recommendation, at least might have suggested to the government that it should leave some money in the hands of the people of Canada so they would be in a position to build their own houses. I have a mortgage on my house. My house is one of the greatest pleasures of my life, even though it will cost me a great deal of money. I will try to keep making the payments until I own every lock, stock and barrel of it. I should like to see every family in Canada own a home at least like mine. It would cost a lot of money, but it should be possible. The governments at all three levels, federal, provincial and municipal, must co-operate. I suggest they could do this by consulting each other in an effort to find out how they might eliminate some of the double and triple taxation. By all means, an effort should be made to eliminate the triple taxation. Why should there be taxes on taxes on taxes? We are paying taxes on our mortgage payments, we are paying taxes on our provincial taxes and we are paying taxes on our municipal taxes.
Taxation can be an ahnost unbearable burden. As a conservative estimate, if you will forgive that word, I believe these three levels of government are taking now in the form of taxes at least 50 per cent of the average person's pay cheque. Once the figure is over the 50 per cent level it is crucial. The other day I read an article which indicated that consumer trade alone in 1968 went up an extra $1 billion, so this means $1 billion less is available. In many cases we are exposed to exorbitant interest rates which results in diminishing returns in business for Canadians. Governments apparently at all levels-and this is nonpartisan because we have Conservative governments in some provinces and Liberal governments in others-are all doing the same thing; they are trying to get a bigger and better share of the taxpayer's dollar in order to do bigger and better works.
March 4. 1969	COMMONS
I believe we are reaching a very dangerous level if we have not 'already gone over the hump. It begins to look like 1928 and 1929. I can tell by the grey hairs that there are a good many members in this house who went through that period. We probably would not survive a second bout of that disease. Let us try to put on the brakes now in respect of government spending at all levels and leave a little money in the hands of the people so they will be able to purchase their own homes. I still think a home is the finest anchor in a free society because one can be proud of it, work for it and be willing to defend it. Then, there is the matter of the exploited land value. Even before thinking of the expense of building a home, many people find they are unable to pay the price for a miserable 50-foot stretch of land. So, we have strike after strike and increase after increase in unemployment.
I should like to see a task force which would give a little more thought to equality of opportunity. Let us not close our eyes to the rising level of unemployment. We blame it on automation. Automation is here to stay and we must make sure it is worked into our society in such a way that the work force will be spread around. This might mean a reduction in hours of labour. The money must be evenly distributed to people and we must make sure that all do their share. Equality of opportunity means the right to share in effort, as well as in the distribution of wealth once the effort is made by other people.
I know, as I am sure the minister knows, that it is not just a simple matter of distributing publicly owned or publicly rented housing all around. The question of housing is infinitely tied up with the matter of transportation. It might well be that we should look into the question of whether or not automobiles should be allowed in the hearts of our major cities. Perhaps we should also look into the matter of rapid transportation systems. It might be considered advisable to keep the gasoline powered motor vehicles out of the hearts of the cities.
As I said, I am inclined to think that the task force did a good job in the limited time they had, but I wonder whether they have gone far enough. I certainly think more consultations could have been held. I am not laying the blame on anyone, but I believe there still are groups of people who might have been consulted. I do not believe we will get anywhere unless we have much greater

subsubtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY-PAYMENT OF INCOME TAX ON GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, February 21, as recorded at page 5797 of Hansard I put this question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson):
In view of the fact that the President of the Privy Council yesterday left a few days in the spring schedule for a budget presentation, will the Minister of Finance take advantage of that opportunity, whether or not he does anything else, to correct the situation under which old age pensioners, when they get the guaranteed income supplement, have to pay income tax?
I was very pleased to receive this answer from the Minister of Finance:
Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to consider the very serious representations of my hon. friend.
I earnestly hope that the consideration the Minister of Finance was prepared to give to my representations will result in his taking action this spring to correct this serious and very unfortunate anomaly in our income tax situation. I am sure it was never intended that people who have only the old age pension to live on should have to pay income tax on any portion of that pension. I am equally sure it was never intended, when the government came through with the idea of a minimum level of income that old age pensioners should have, that having given that minimum with one hand part of it would be taken away with the other; but for pensioners between 65 and 70 that is the result under the legislation as it now stands.
March 4, 1969

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I should like to use a few figures, and I shall use those which apply to 1968 because pensioners who are now faced with this situation have to pay income tax in April, 1969, on the basis of what they received in 1968.
If a single pensioner in 1968 received the full amount of the pension plus the full amount of the guaranteed income supplement his total income for the year was $1,285.20. If he was between the ages of 65 and 70 this means that his total exemption allowed would be $1,100; $1,000 plus the standard $100 for charitable donations. That would mean that he had to pay income tax on $185.20, which would mean that on last year's income he would have to pay $23.70 income tax. In other words, he would pay a tax of almost $2 a month which would wipe out the $2 a month he received because of the cost of living increase.
A married couple between 65 and 70 years of age, at least if the taxpayer was in that age bracket, who desired to report their income as a married couple, if both of them were getting the guaranteed income supplement, would receive $2,570.40 in 1968, but because the wife was in receipt of an income in excess of $250 the husband's total exemption would be only $1,100.00 and he would have to pay taxes on $1,470.40. His tax would be over $215. That couple could report their incomes as two single persons and cut off a certain amount, but they would still have to pay $23.70 each.
I am sure that even though the former Minister of Finance defended this when I complained about it some time ago, this was not the intent. Let me cite also the kind of case that is coming to my attention these days in relation to persons on pensions from private sources of say $1,200 a year. Such a person receives in old age pension $900 a year which brings him up to $2,100. That individual's income tax exemption is $1,000 plus $100 charitable donation, plus $1,000 for his wife, so he paid no income tax. If his wife happened to be a year or two younger, when she moved into the pension age bracket, she would receive $900, or $918 as it was last year.
This would bring the total income for such a couple to a little over $3,000. Because the wife had an income of $918 last year the exemption her husband would be allowed for her would only be $332, so his total exemption is $1,000 plus $100 for charitable donations, plus $332. He would have only $1,432

exemption which would mean he would have to pay income tax on the rest, and this would amount to $238.
The fact that this man's wife received a pension of $918 last year would mean that he has to pay a tax of $238. Surely, rates like this are unconscionable if deliberate. I suggest they were accidental. I draw the minister's attention to the fact that the present exemption rates of $1,000 for single people and $2,000 for married couples were set in 1949, 20 years ago. At the beginning of that year the old age pension was $30 per month. Later that year it was raised to $40 per month. In the years when those income tax exemptions were set those people had no problem. As time has passed and pensions have gone up from $30 to $40 to $75, to $105 and to $109 these exemptions have not been raised.
Because nothing has been done about these exemption levels, I submit that an 'anomalous situation now exists in respect of people from 65 to 70. I feel very strongly about this. Time will not permit me to say anything more about the situation tonight, but I hope the minister will deal with this anomaly this spring, without fail.

subsubtopic: DRUGS-MACE-TESTS TO REVEAL POSSIBLE DANGERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 3, I directed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) in connection with tests carried out on the chemical Mace. I asked the minister whether he would consider making a statement regarding any experiments his department might have conducted on the use of the chemical. The minister replied that he had had an opportunity of looking into this matter. He said that as far as he was aware it was not being used by any of the law enforcement units in Canada.
While the minister's reply gave me some information, it did not really answer the basic question that I put to him. The question was whether the department was conducting experiments and, if so, whether a report had been issued or information was available on the use of this chemical. The minister's reply, that as far as he knew there were not any law enforcement units in Canada using the chemical may have been somewhat misleading. It might have left the impression that police units were not considering the use of the chemical Mace or did not have the chemical at their disposal. According to reports of suppliers of the chemical, at least 35 Canadian police forces have the chemical. If they have gone to the trouble of obtaining the chemical, one must assume they are prepared to use it.
Representations have been made on the use of the chemical, and criticism has come from many quarters. The B.C. Civil Liberties Association said that Mace is an offence against civil liberties. The B.C. Association of Social Workers said that more research is needed on its effect. The Vancouver Labour Council passed a resolution condemning the chemical Mace. Public agencies throughout the country have pointed out the dangers of the use of the chemical.
I am not in a position to really know what are the effects of the use of the chemical, but a sufficient number of questions has been raised to indicate that the Department of National Health and Welfare is under an obligation to make a statement indicating whether or not it has tested the chemical. It should let the public know to what extent the chemical is, or is not, dangerous. This was my purpose in asking for an adjournment debate tonight on this subject. I hope the parliamentary secretary, who is here to speak on behalf of the minister, can at this time indicate what

Regard must be paid to the fact that those who recruit players for this club have to compete with the National Hockey League for the talent they wish to attract. In these circumstances, it is very difficult under our present system for Canada to get a club which is capable of beating teams representing certain European nations.
I, for one, am not too disturbed because we have not been able to beat clubs from Russia and Czechoslovakia. As everyone knows, we are playing their best but we are not using our best. As I have often said, if the day comes when Russia has a professional hockey organization such as operates in North America, and we play the teams which do not qualify to play in their professional hockey association, I do not think there is any doubt we could beat those clubs with the type of club we are sending across today.
I point out to the minister that another meeting is being held this Friday in Toronto, and I submit that representatives of the Canadian Hockey Association should be specifically invited to attend. Although it is recognized that the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association is the governing body in amateur hockey, and has been for many years, times have changed in Canada. We now have in existence this new Canadian Hockey Association. At the present time seven of the players on our national hockey team have played in the western Canada hockey league which is now under the jurisdiction of this Canadian Hockey Association.
It is also common knowledge, if one talks to scouts for the National Hockey League teams, that in the opinion of these scouts ten or 11 of the top junior hockey players in Canada are playing under the banner of the Canadian Hockey Association. These are not my figures; these are the figures of the scouts for the National Hockey League.
I should also like to refer to one or two other matters in order to try to impress upon the minister the desirability of having


representatives from the Canadian Hockey Association attend these meetings. If people are going to sit down and hold a round table discussion on how to improve our national hockey team, then I think it is only advisable to have present the people who are operating some of the clubs that might be expected to contribute players.
For example, I can safely say there are players in the western Canada hockey league today who will be able to assist our national hockey team in its planned trips overseas. However, the representatives of these hockey players are not even being invited to sit down with a group of people whom the minister, or someone, has called together to discuss this important subject.
I understand representatives of the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association are being invited to the meeting. They were invited to the last one and they are probably being invited next Friday. I also understand there will be representatives from at least two National Hockey League clubs. I assume there will be representatives from Canada's fitness council. Why should there not be present representatives from the Canadian Hockey Association who are operating a strong league in western Canada consisting of over 160 junior players, and who also operate a league in eastern Canada that consists of some 120 junior players?
I am not saying that these clubs would be able to make available immediately players to assist our national team. However, if representatives of this association were invited to sit down at a round table conference of the type envisaged, I think they could put forward some ideas for assisting our national hockey team.
In closing, I should also like to mention that it is apparent that the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association has in some manner blacklisted the Canadian Hockey Association simply because it has not operated fully within the rules and regulations laid down by the C.A.H.A. I give the Canadian Hockey Association credit for one thing: they have decided to operate on their own for one specific reason, namely, that they contend junior hockey players should be at least 21 years of age. The C.A.H.A. requires a player to be under 20 years of age to play junior hockey. In the days when there was a good brand of senior hockey played all across Canada, perhaps this provision was quite acceptable. Now we have all these various pro leagues, the time has come when we should have junior hockey-

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Hockey Association was not represented. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association is the officially recognized body by the International Ice Hockey Association. Any player who plays for Canada must be on the C.A.H.A. list. Because the Canadian Hockey Association is a breakaway organization, players within their jurisdiction are not on the C.A.H.A. lists. This is a potentially difficult situation and it is the wish of all Canadians interested in our
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion national team that arrangements can be worked out so that the best possible national team can be put forward.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has not interceded in what is basically a family quarrel. I would mention though that the Hockey Canada meetings were very representative. Members from the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association, Canada Intercollegiate Athletic Union, Professional Hockey and Professional Hockey Players Associations were represented, together with the government and the public spirited hockey fans who, I am confident, will help to make Hockey Canada a success.
